subtopic: SALVATION ARMY ACT, 1989 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to make some comments on this particular bill.
The organization that is the subject of this particular bill is represented very strongly across Canada. In fact, I did some research on its background. It is a very rich background that I will not go through here, although I think it is worth while to recall some of the dates involved, to give some indication of just how steeped in our history the organization called The Salvation Army is.
It first came to Canada in 1882. It was introduced by a group of very dedicated people. The corps first really sprung up in smaller towns in Ontario.
As an indication of the kind of movement that the Salvation Army had, just five years later the religion, as I would prefer to call it, was being practised from Victoria, British Columbia to St. John's, Newfoundland. In relative terms, that was a very short time for a religion or a particular movement to spread across any country.
There are a number of milestones worth pointing out. In 1886, the organization was a rescue home for fallen girls, as it was called. In 1891, the Salvation Army opened its first prison-gate home. In 1905, a Salvation Army officer became the first Dominion Parole Officer.
This is an organization of great stature in our country. Today, the Salvation Army maintains both a social and a religious or evangelical purpose. It is a recognized church with close to 130,000 members.
In my travels across Canada, in the Bermuda area and other parts of the world, I have been very impressed with the kind of work the Salvation Army does. If I may be permitted a personal aside, the very first duty I had to perform after being elected in the riding of Bonavista- Trinity-Conception was to attend a dinner given by the

March 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
Salvation Army in my hometown of Bonavista. It was at that dinner that I committed my assistance to the movement and some of the projects it is interested in because of my belief, faith, and the way I have been touched by what it has done in its time in Canada, especially in the smaller villages and towns of Newfoundland where the movement is particularly strong.
Across Canada there are parole supervision agencies, the well-known Harbour Light Centre for alcoholics, Sunset Lodges, Grace Hospitals, fresh air camps for youngsters and programs for drug addicts. In my riding there are two camps which the Salvation Army through hard work has put together. It continues to supervise the youth activities. In fact, some of these camps double for activities which involve senior citizens and other like organizations of a recreational nature.
To summarize, the indication that the Salvation Army has put across is that it is a willing hand in a time of need. I am familiar, as I am sure anybody who has been associated with the organization is, with its motto, "With heart to God and hand to man". I think all of us have a lot of time for the kind of work that this particular organization does. It is for that reason that it has such great stature in our country.
My concern in reviewing the information that I had on this bill was that we simply did not make amendments to an existing organization that could come back and perhaps make life difficult for the Salvation Army. I just had to review for my own benefit precisely what this amendment was doing.
The Salvation Army as a church has what is called the core managing board, which does not have the ownership of the property within which it performs its function. All that ownership rests with the corporation which is called the governing council of the Salvation Army. In simplistic terms, I understand that this council has to be set up in order to have ownership of the property and the many organizations which represent real estate to which I have made reference. This is opposed to the Salvation Army movement itself, which as a religious movement would not have title to these particular properties.
The governing council was split in two in 1916 when there was formed a separate territory called the Canada West in Winnipeg, which was a special regional organization.
In 1930, because of severe economic conditions and, once more, because of the business of trying to amalgamate and save administrative dollars, the army amalgamated this group. The senior leadership moved to one centre in Toronto without having made the change in the legislation.
In simple terms the legislation, as I understand it, has never caught up with the reality of the reorganization that took place in 1930. The officers of the governing council are the same for Canada West and Canada East. For purposes of tightening up the structure and ensuring the tidying up of the corporate legislative details, the Salvation Army brought forward this bill, which it hopes to see passed as soon as possible.
It is my privilege on behalf of my colleagues, and I hope all members of the House, to say that any reservations we had have been discharged. I hope that in passing this bill we will allow an organization that is running for the good of mankind to run a bit more smoothly from the administrative and legislative side. We are quite happy to proceed with this bill.

Second, on behalf of all members of this House, I wish to say how much we appreciate the work of the Salvation Army or, as it is more affectionately called, the Sally Ann. It has definitely created an attitude in this country of credibility, of kindness and a spirit that all of us would do well to imitate and reflect upon.
I often think of one soldier I talked to who is about as hard and cynical a man as I know who regularly referred so kindly to the Sally Ann officers who had cared for him and helped him during the times of war.
I also want to say that I appreciate the co-operation of both the Liberal and NDP members and how much they have helped us in proceeding with this bill. I know that the House does want to express to the Salvation Army our continued support for its work and our appreciation for what it does for so many Canadians who, from time to time have suffered hardship. It has demonstrated leadership.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have had it with the government's misguided industrial policy that makes them victims of a rather perverse economic strategy. More workers lost their jobs through layoffs last year than in any other year since 1982. That alarming increase in plant closings means that over 9,700 jobs lost last year will be gone for good.
Moreover, anticipated workforce reductions is greater than in any similar period during the last decade. To make matters worse, new jobs in generally low paying service sectors accounted for 93.7 per cent of all jobs created.
More and more Canadians are forced to take on additional part-time jobs to make ends meet. Those holding such jobs increased by over 45 per cent in the last 10 years. Good jobs are being lost and little is being done to replace them.
The 550 workers at Inglis in Toronto are a case in point. Fewer than 100 have found jobs since the plant moved operations to Ohio. Where are the adjustment policies for them? Where is the industrial strategy to reintegrate them into the economy? They and others want work. Why is the government deliberately creating conditions for increased unemployment?

Mr. Speaker, Canada has started implementing an environmental clean-up program in the Arctic.
About 5,000 old fuel drums were collected and shipped south, as part of the first clean-up phase.
General waste management practices in the Arctic are now being reviewed. The federal government will consider and test practical methods for waste reduction, waste treatment, incineration, recycling and waste removal.
There is a wide variety of activities in Canada's North isolated though it may be.
Environment Canada maintains a network of weather stations, air pollution monitoring posts and a national park reserve.
Now that research has shown that air pollution from the temperate zones is now contaminating the far North, Canada is trying to deal with pollution on a much broader scale.
For instance, the federal government has concluded co-operation agreements with the U.S.S.R. concerning the Arctic, reduction of air pollution and environmental problems in general.
Mr. Speaker, we are now working on a new agreement with all Arctic countries in order better to protect the environment in the North.

Mr. Speaker, there was very good news from Ottawa for Canadians this past weekend. Because it was good news, it did not show in the headlines.
This February, employment increased and unemployment actually decreased to 7.7 per cent, even though February is usually a low point in the labour cycle. Two conclusions can be drawn from this. First, while Canadians may not be enjoying boom times right now, we have not had to face the severe recession that many have been predicting.

March 12, 1990
Second, we should all remember that when the previous Liberal government left office in September 1984, usually a month of maximum employment, the unemployment rate was 11.6 per cent. Now, the unemployment rate is down to 7.7 per cent in mid-winter. What this proves is that whatever the doomsayers and negative nigglers might say during Question Period, this government is following the proper economic course for Canadians. Also, any connection between headlines and reality is slim, at best.

Mr. Speaker, the most severe forest fires to hit Canada this century happened last summer in northern Manitoba. In all, 2.6 million hectares of land burned in Manitoba. Forests, lakes and wildlife population were all devastated. There were 23,000 people evacuated from their homes and communities. At that time, the Prime Minister went on record on television with an offer of generous help from Ottawa. He said Ottawa would help to cover the enormous cost of fighting fires and evacuating people.
I want Canadians to know that now that the bills are coming in, the Prime Minister is backing off. The fires in 1989 cost the people of Manitoba $72 million. Under normal disaster relief formulas, Ottawa should pay half of that cost, which amounts to over $36 million. Instead, the Prime Minister is offering to pay only $17 million.
What happened to the Prime Minister's generosity? Did it vanish when the cameras were turned off? There is no question that Ottawa should pay its fair and generous share of the cost of fighting last summer's fires as promised. The people of Manitoba, after all, are still watching and they will not forget.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women is holding its annual symposium today and tomorrow on the theme of Women's Place in the Economy. The President of the council says: "We are at a crisis point.
Women are under siege". The President of the National Employment Network, calls this an anti-woman government on the attack to the feminist movement.
This is a good time to recall the record of this government on issues that keep women poor. A national day care program has been abandoned. Bill C-21 cuts unemployment benefits and hurts women disproportionately. The Minister responsible for the Status of Women refuses to accept an amendment that would have given equal access to training programs for women.
The government, which should be leading the way in enlightened employment and pay policies, instead is perpetuating sexual stereotyping and negative attitudes. It hurts women by withholding pension reforms that are its obligation under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. For months it has left the Court Challenges Program in limbo. After cuts last year to women's programs, the latest blow is the slashing of federal funding to women's centres while hundreds of thousands of women across this country are beaten daily. Women are not deceived by empty rhetoric. They want action.

Mr. Speaker, the sports community is reacting to the "English-only" trend, and Quebec francophones involved in cross-country skiing feel very strongly they have been humiliated.
At a committee meeting, it was decided that from now on, Quebec would withdraw and stay away from all competitions, whatever their size, held in cities that had passed unilingual resolutions.
The city of Sault Ste. Marie, which has given the "English-only" trend new importance, hosted a Canadian championship two years ago. In the present circumstances, the winner, Pierre Harvey, would have been unable to take part.
The Quebec federation wants to remind the Canadian association it has a duty to ensure that Quebec is respected as a province. In future, it will be up to the executive to make sure it selects sites where our rights will not be trampled on.
March 12, 1990

Mr. Speaker, last summer I attended the Saskatoon Games where I saw a fantastic organization that functioned in both official languages.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that this week, throughout Canada, around the clock, Canadian men and women will dial 1-900-720-6052 to object to the goods and services tax.
I urge Canadians to support the national campaign against the goods and services tax which will take place from March 12 to March 16.
This telephone petition will enable all Canadians to vote against the GST and express their dissatisfaction. Vote massively againts the GST!
Say no to the GST by dialing 1-900-720-6052.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House the issue of acid rain. Last June the President of the United States, George Bush, introduced legislation that would see acid rain emissions from industrial sources cut back nearly half by the turn of the century.
More recently the United States stated in principle that they were ready to agree to that legislation after successful negotiations were completed between the White House and the Senate. This is only the latest in the long list of successes for our government since 1984 on the issue of acid rain.
Our own country set a prime example. Agreements were made with the provinces affected by acid rain to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions by 2.3 million tonnes per year. Lead is to be removed from gasoline emissions by December 1, 1990. New emission standards have reduced the amount of pollution from cars and trucks. The list goes on.
This is evidence that all the time and effort put forth by this government and especially by our Prime Minister to address this problem to the President of the United States is finally meeting with success. Only by Canadians
and Americans working toward the common goal of acid rain reform can we realize a cleaner, healthier environment for all North Americans.

Mr. Speaker, today my colleagues and I met with representatives of labour groups from across this country. They brought the message once again that the government's plan to destroy unemployment insurance will not be accepted.
The government's response to the Senate does nothing to respond to the serious concerns of people from across the country who have appeared before committee after committee.
Bill C-21 is bad legislation. At the very time when workers most need income protection, whether they live in Canso or Saskatoon, the government is cutting benefits and increasing hardships for thousands of families.
The Senate amendments do not go nearly far enough toward maintaining the kind of program this country so desperately needs. This government should listen to the people, do the honourable thing and withdraw this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard from friends and fellow members of the Ogden Branch of the Royal Canadian Legion who support recent changes to the board and lodging charges for long term care for Canada's veterans. They know that these changes correct an inequity where the majority of veterans pay $240 a month while others pay nothing for the same service.
Veterans across the country will now be treated equally. Veterans with low incomes or disability will pay less than $240 a month or nothing at all. Veterans will continue to pay the lowest rate for long term care in Canada because the maximum amount is set at the lowest rate charged by any province. These changes do not affect veterans' pensions and allowances which continue to be generous and fully indexed. For example, married veterans are guaranteed $1,185 a month before deductions, and single veterans are guaranteed $585 a month before deductions. Veterans also receive Old Age

Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate Commonwealth Day and it is very fitting that we welcome the joining of Namibia on March 21 as the fiftieth member of the Commonwealth.
Her Majesty, The Queen, is head of the Commonwealth. I would like to read two brief paragraphs from her message:
Every year, when we celebrate Commonwealth Day, it reminds me that we are celebrating something which is quite unique. Nothing quite like the Commonwealth has ever been created or evolved before. Its comparative lack of rules, its human richness and its geographical diversity, make the Commonwealth as hard to define as it is easy to criticize-it appeals to the young as much as to the old, to peoples and nations at all phases of political, economic, cultural and social development, to reformers and lovers of tradition alike.
On Commonwealth Day especially we greet each other as members of the biggest and most unusual family on earth.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister and it relates to the government's policy for improving Canada's science and technology performance, in particular the role to be played by the National Research Council of Canada.
The new president of the NRC wrote last month to the Chair of the Science Council that the National Research Council: "intends to limit its involvement in basic research-to that required to maintain a minimal scientific insurance policy for the nation".
Does the Acting Prime Minister agree with his new NRC president that the NRC should play a minimal role in science and, at this time in Canada's history, why is the government forcing the NRC to play such a minimal role?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is not forcing the National Research Council to do anything. The National Research Council is doing exactly what it should do. It should review its mandate from time to time. It should recog-

nize that universities now exist and are the main thrust for basic scientific work in this country. The National Research Council will do what is required in terms of basic research so that it can fulfil its general mandate to support science and technology in this country.

I hope the minister has heard about the transfer cuts.

Mr. Speaker, in the same letter, Dr. Perron, president of the NRC, proposes a policy and strategy for privatization of the National Research Council. Is the government prepared to let the National Research Council be privatized?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):

Mr. Speaker, the National Research Council of Canada is not going to be privatized.
I think what may hurt my colleague so much is that the National Research Council of Canada is prepared to sell some of its services to industry if industry wants to buy it. That seems to me to be a good deal.

Mr. Speaker, if that is the policy of the government, I suggest that the minister head the president of the NRC off at the pass when he is writing letters that say he is proposing a policy of privatization.
As recently as the budget last month, the government cut science and technology spending by $39 million and cut transfer payments for post-secondary education by over $2 billion. Canadians are left wondering what has happened to the Prime Minister's promise of increasing Canada's R and D spending to 2.5 per cent of Gross Domestic Product?
Does the government still intend to fulfil the Prime Minister's promise to increase R and D spending to 2.5 per cent and, if so, can the government explain how it intends to increase R and D performance while cutting spending?

of it. Let me remind the hon. member that in 1980, the government of the day was spending, excluding debt payments, 4.65 per cent of total program spending on science and technology. Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and pertains to the historical events happening in Lithuania.
It is clear that the situation in the Baltic States is very different, indeed very unique from that of the other republics in the Soviet Union. Successive governments have refused to recognize the illegal annexation of those states.
Will the minister bring a long-standing policy of non-recognition to its logical conclusion by supporting an all-party resolution that recognizes Lithuania as a fully independent, sovereign republic? I can tell the minister that I have had discussions with the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona and he, on behalf of his party, would be willing to support such a resolution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity to look at the resolution that was proposed by the hon. member and the member for Winnipeg Transcona. Certainly, that would be a resolution that would be acceptable to me and to members of the government.
We join with the hon. member in recognizing as historic the democratic decision that has been taken by the people of Lithuania, and now by their Parliament. The position of the Government of Canada, as he has correctly said, has been to recognize the political sovereignty of Lithuania.
We now enter into a very important phase in which there will be a discussion as to how the de facto occupation by the Soviet Union will come to an end.

March 12, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for that co-operation and leadership. I am wondering if he could go a step further because yesterday my riding which was linked by telephone to Vilnius where the newly elected Lithuanian Parliament voted unanimously to change the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic to become the independent democratic Republic of Lithuania.
In addition to the resolution, would the minister today give full recognition to the Republic of Lithuania by giving it full diplomatic recognition?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House was pleased that the hon. member, his colleague from Winnipeg Transcona, and the member for Scarborough Centre were able, in private capacities, to be in Lithuania to watch the elections and report back to their caucuses.
I have had some conversations with some of the members respecting those developments. This is an historic day. I have discussed with Soviet leaders, prior to the vote, the attitude that they would take.
I have received specifically from Mr. Shevardnadze can undertaking that there would be no crackdown. I think all members of the House would agree that we should encourage the Soviet Union and Lithuania to move as speedily as possible toward a situation which recognizes the de facto and de jure sovereignty and independence of Lithuania.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for Science who has been recently elevated, for which I congratulate him.
I wonder if he would elevate himself to answer this question. The Prime Minister is to receive an award tonight for scientific leadership from the Weizmann Institute.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, those on the other side seem well informed. Perhaps they can tell us why this award was received. Is it for cutting Canadian expenditures for research as a percentage of the Gross Domestic Product from 1.4 per cent in 1985 to 1.32 per cent in
1989? Is it for cutting the government's share of science and technology expenditures by 4 per cent over four years? Or is it for cutting the EPF transfers in support of universities? Which of these constitutes scientific leadership?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his congratulations. In turn, I would like to congratulate the Prime Minister on receiving this award.
There are no doubt many reasons why the institute decided to award the Prime Minister this distinguished award, many of them no doubt are centred on the fact that this is a Prime Minister who established the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology and chairs it for the first time ever in Canadian history.
This is the Prime Minister who, working with that board, established the Canada Scholarship Program, the Centres of Excellence Program, and who managed to put in $350 million or more into the industry-university matching grant program. This is the Prime Minister who ensured, as I said to my hon. colleague just a moment ago, that we went from 4.46 per cent in 1984 to 4.89 per cent of total program expenditure on science and technology in 1989. That is not a bad record.

Mr. Speaker, the quality of excuses is not strained, and I can understand why there was such a lack of enthusiasm on the other side with respect to the award. But let us look at the record.
On February 8, the parliamentary secretary to the hon. minister promised that there would be no new cut-backs at NRC.
What is the supplementary?

Do not get too agitated over there, you will get your turn some other time. We have a document to which my colleague in the Official Opposition referred which states that in this correspondence between the head of the NRC and the former head of the Science Council the next five year plan for NRC will propose a strategy of privatization and divestiture and planned reductions in permanent employees at NRC. How can he reconcile that to the statement of the parliamentary secretary to the hon. minister and to any significant thrust in the direction of building up Canada's R and D capacity?
March 12, 1990

That is exactly what they are looking at.
I am amazed that the opposition does not want to see the National Research Council look at its future in terms of the reality of the present, but then it has never been one to face reality.

I indicated last Friday that until such time as there appeared to be some move toward greater consensus among the divergent views of the three opposing provinces it would seem rather untimely to bring all the ministers together under the auspices of a First Ministers' Conference. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I have the pleasure of joining with members from all sides of the House and one-quarter of the world's people in observing Commonwealth Day.
The modem Commonwealth has been central to the growth of Canada's role in the world and remains a key element in its external relations. It gives Canada partners in Asia and Africa with whom it shares a heritage of British political and legal traditions, and with whom it can communicate through the English language. It strengthens historical ties with the English-speaking Caribbean and widens ties in the Pacific. It deepens our understanding of the problems of developing countries and provides the opportunity to make an important contribution to technical and development assistance. It also provides inspiration for Canada to seek parallel institutions which would cement ties in the Frenchspeaking world.
Canada's annual contribution of some $40 million to official Commonwealth organizations chiefly serves to assist developing and particularly the smaller countries of the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth connection facilitates Canada's own development aid program and the effective use of Canadian aid. In 1989-90, Canada will have directed close to $1 billion of bilateral and multilateral development assistance to some 50 Commonwealth countries or territories.
I also wish to draw special attention to the Commonwealth Distance Learning Agency based in Vancouver. This Commonwealth collaboration in distance education, created through a Canadian initiative at the 1987 Commonwealth heads of government meeting, promotes the exchange of information, training, technical assistance, and research in the application of distance education techniques at post-secondary and vocational levels in the developing Commonwealth countries.
;

The meeting of the Commonwealth heads of government in Kuala Lumpur last October reviewed the multi-faceted activities of the organization and addressed major international political and economic issues ranging from the situation in the Middle East to the world economic situation and the full integration of women in all aspects of economic, social and political life.
To further the Commonwealth's work toward gender equality, Canada will host the third meeting of Commonwealth Ministers Responsible for Women's Affairs. I am pleased and honoured to be able to welcome my counterparts from other countries to this meeting. In the spirit of Commonwealth co-operation, we will continue to work on issues such as structural adjustment and violence against women.

The meeting in Kuala Lumpur showed that the Commonwealth not only holds consultations on the major world issues but also takes concerted action to deal with them.

Considering recent events in South Africa, due credit has to be given to the leading role played by the Commonwealth in pressing for the opening that we are witnessing, particularly the unbanning of the African National Congress and the release of Nelson Mandela which we so heartily welcome. At Kuala Lumpur, heads of government expressed their hope for a negotiated and peaceful settlement in southern Africa and agreed to the maintenance of existing sanctions as a way of exerting continued pressure for fundamental political change.
I also want to take advantage of this occasion to praise the Canadian delegation which contributed so wonderfully to the enhancement of Canada's image at the recent Commonwealth Games in Auckland. I am particularly happy that Canada will remain active in this strengthening of Commonwealth sports through its participation and chairmanship in the working party that has been constituted by the Commonwealth Secretary-General. We look forward to hosting the 1994 Commonwealth Games in Victoria, British Columbia.
We all rejoice in the return of Pakistan to the Commonwealth last October, which can only strengthen Commonwealth collaborative action. In addition, Na-

mibia's imminent entry, which will bring Commonwealth membership to 50, serves to reaffirm the value and relevance of the modem Commonwealth.
I have left to the end the tribute that I would like to pay to Secretary-General Ramphal. He will be relinquishing his post at the end of June after 15 years in office. Sonny Ramphal's leadership and devotion proudly strengthened the Commonwealth and its contribution to international stability, progress and justice. We are all in his debt and we wish him well.
Finally, I want to reiterate this government's support to Sonny Ramphal's successor, Chief Emeka Anyaoku, whose extensive record of effective service to the Commonwealth portends a mandate of achievement and success in the year's to come.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to deliver a statement on the Commonwealth on this special day of honouring it as an international organization.
The Commonwealth is a very unusual international organization. Once an empire, it has become an institution comprised of nearly one-quarter of the world's population. Almost every race, religious faith, culture and level of economic development can be found in the Commonwealth fold. Composed of 50 independent states, its members range from aligned to non-aligned and have all shades of ideological opinion.
The Commonwealth is an essentially multinational body of equal sovereign members with a common concern for international peace and a commitment to the economic development of member countries. Consultation and co-operation govern this association.
The Commonwealth's ties are informal and diverse. It possesses none of the attributes generally attached to an international political association. There is no constitution. The association does not encroach on the sovereignty of individual members, it has no common foreign policy and does not require its members to reach collective decisions or to take united action. There is nothing formally or legally binding the member states together.
Yet the Commonwealth is a very compatible organization. This can be traced to the fact that all member states were former British colonies in one way or another. Members share the basic traditions of respect for the

Routine Proceedings
British parliamentary democracy, the rule of law and the rights of individuals and minorities.
The Commonwealth has been doing for years what similar organizations are just starting to accept and to implement. Members do not strive to solve political problems, but work towards reducing strains and easing tensions in order to provide a framework in which differences can begin to be reconciled. The Commonwealth if definitely given to practicality. It can deal as effectively with the great problems of the day as it can with everyday problems.
The heads of government in the Commonwealth meet on a regular basis. These meetings are often the testing grounds for ideas. The results of such meetings are often noteworthy. For instance, the Declaration of Commonwealth Principles and the establishment of a fund for technical co-operation in 1971, the Lusaka declaration of 1979 opposing racism and racial prejudice, and the Melbourne declaration of 1981 expressing a determination to end global poverty and inequality.
Countries small and large have a voice within the Commonwealth. Twenty-six member states have populations that number less than one million. The Commonwealth is often the most significant link these countries have with the rest of the world. The Commonwealth is, as a result, the best advocate for the special needs and problems of these small countries. As virtually every region of the world is represented in the Commonwealth, it is easy to see that membership helps more than it hinders.
"India has contacts with southeast Asian states which no other Commonwealth country can match. Canada has an unrivalled knowledge of the United States; Britain has knowledge of Europe. Jamaica has a special advantage in understanding the countries of the Caribbean" and so can advises others. This becomes important as we move towards increasing global trade.
Both Canada and the Commonwealth have benefited from our membership. Not only have we helped to preserve the association in times of crisis and supported
all its programs, but we have been led to change some of our attitudes, especially those towards the Third World.
I recall attending a Caribbean Commonwealth Conference in 1973 as an observer with two former MPs, Senator Heath Macquarrie and the present Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, Lincoln Alexander. At the beginning of the conference, the chairman stood up and said: "We want our three Canadian friends who are here as observers to feel free to intervene in our proceedings any time they wish to speak, for Canada is the best friend the Caribbean Commonwealth countries have in the world. Great Britain is next. And after that we don't even enumerate them."
On that trip, I flew to a cadet training camp to visit with 30 Canadian cadets who were there to train for a month with other cadets from Commonwealth countries. The Jamaican pilot who flew me in informed me that he had received his training at Portage la Prairie in Manitoba. This is just another concrete example of the co-operation that goes on within the Commonwealth.
On that same day, we received word that the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent had passed away. I brought this to the attention of the chairman of the Caribbean meeting and the first item of business was a moment of silence in his honour. One could sense the sincerity and the warm feeling extended towards Canada.
In a world where division often reigns according to ideology, race, region, level of economic development or religion, the Commonwealth is necessary. It manages to ignore group interest and help bring about a global solution to common problems. The Commonwealth is proof that through consensus a great deal can be achieved. Prime Minister Nehru of India's statement in 1949 sums it up perfectly: the Commonwealth "brings a healing touch to a sick world."
Today we extend our best wishes to the other 49 members of the modem day Commonwealth. We extend the hand of friendship and co-operation to them in order to continue to help them make the Commonwealth a great human and political organization, and an outstanding example of international co-operation and friendship for the entire world.
March 12, 1990

The Commonwealth has a tremendous amount of wealth of knowledge and understanding to offer to the rest of the world and is a great basic factor in pulling various peoples of the world together in harmony.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to rise on behalf of my party and pay tribute to the Commonwealth on this Commonwealth Day, and to pick up where the minister speaking for the government left off when she extended her congratulations to Sonny Ramphal, the Secretary-General of the Commonwealth, for the work that he has done over the years. Mr. Ramphal is to retire, and we wish his successor well.
However, I also want to note in a personal way that I had the opportunity to hear Mr. Ramphal on a number of occasions and have always found his speeches and his analyses of the global situation to be among the best that I have ever heard. I listened to him last October at the annual meeting of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. I would recommend that speech to the minister and to all ministers of the government, because its analyses of the global environmental situation and what needs to be done, and done in a hurry, runs contrary to the policies of the government. It is one thing to congratulate Mr. Ramphal; it is another thing to pay attention to what he has to say. I would hope that someday we might see that kind of attention being paid to the policies which Mr. Ramphal advocated.
I am thinking particularly of the greenhouse effect and his concern about that, but also his concern about another Commonwealth country, Bangladesh, which stands to suffer a calamity if all the predictions about greenhouse warming and rising of the sea level are true. The delegates from Bangladesh become desperate when they contemplate what the possible consequences of the greenhouse effect might be. We should keep then-situation in mind when we are making decisions about hydrocarbon policy and various other things to which this government does not yet seemed to have caught on.
The British Commonwealth is the outcome of a process of decolonization. It is basically what is left over after the decolonization of all the former British colonies. As the hon. member indicated earlier, all members of the Commonwealth, with the exception of Britain, were formerly British colonies. What we need to keep in mind when we think about the Commonwealth, is that decolonization does not have to be the end of relation-
Routine Proceedings
ships. There can be constructive ways for former colonial countries to relate to their now decolonized neighbours or, for that matter, distant neighbours.
The process of decolonization with respect to the Commonwealth is completed with the independence of Namibia, something which all of us welcome and which a number of us have had an opportunity to comment on in the House.
The process of decolonization outside the British Commonwealth has not been completed. In fact, there are new and more recent forms of colonization that have to be addressed, whether it is the colonization of East Timor by Indonesia or Tibet by China. There are numerous examples of existing colonization, to which at this particular time in history, we should be turning our attention. Why not make it a clean slate, and let us pass into a new era of history in which nations are no longer colonies of other nations.
Presumably, later we will have an opportunity to pass a resolution with respect to Lithuania. I would invite Soviet leaders and politicians to think about new ways in which they might relate to the various parts of what has been called their empire, whether or not that is the appropriate way to describe it.
It seems to me that all those things should to be considered when thinking about the Commonwealth.
One of the things that I hope for the British Commonwealth as progress is made in South Africa, assuming that progress comes to fruition and we see the creation of a democratic, non-racial democracy in South Africa, is that then the Commonwealth might be able to turn its attention to other regimes in the Commonwealth, which have literally got away with murder. While every one has been preoccupied with South Africa, there is not a member of Parliament who has not been approached at one time or another about political oppression in various Commonwealth countries.
It does not serve anyone well to have the sort of idyllic view of the Commonwealth that was expressed just before me about this being a group of nations that respect British parliamentary tradition and British law, and all those sorts of things. That would be nice, except the fact of the matter is that in many of these countries in Africa and Asia, these kinds of things are not respected. I hope that soon the Commonwealth will proceed to a point where no longer will we turn a blind eye to some of these things and begin to address the

March 12, 1990
Routine Proceedings
human rights violations that are going on in various Commonwealth countries.
For example, I am reminded of the persecution of Ahmadi Muslims in Pakistan. The minister raised the question of Pakistan's re-entry into the Commonwealth. I think this is a good thing. It is also an opportunity for members of the Commonwealth to express to Prime Minister Bhutto and to others that the kinds of things which are going on in Pakistan with respect to the Ahmadi Muslims are unacceptable to Canadians, as are many other things that are being perpetrated by other Commonwealth countries.
The Commonwealth serves the purpose of being an opportunity to get together, to have an entirely different form of forum for communication and sharing of concerns, but it also ought to be a place where various governments are challenged, not in a self-righteous way, but challenged to live up to the very ideals which the Commonwealth itself says it holds dear. I would hope that the government would see its way to continue to use the Commonwealth in that way.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State to Prime Minister and Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to initiate the response from the government to the message from the other place respecting Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Government Orders
The message from the other place came back with some nine amendments. On behalf of the government I have to state that it objects to several amendments proposed by the Senate because it guts the bill, violate its principles approved by the Commons and it transgresses accepted constitutional boundaries of the Senate's role on government bills coming from the Commons.
First, I would like to note Standing Orders 79 and 80 of our House and Sections 53 and 54 of the Constitution Act, formerly the British North America Act.
Standing Order 79(1) of the House of Commons, which has been in place since Confederation states, and I quote:
This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message from the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.
This simply states the long standing constitutional precedent that a Royal recommendation dictates and must precede any appropriation of funds and any deviation from that by way of amendments would, in fact, be out of order and not permissible under that Standing Order.
Standing Order 79(2) states, and I quote:
The message and recommendation of the Governor General in relation to any bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or of any tax or impost shall be printed on the Notice Paper and in the Votes and Proceedings when any such measure is to be introduced and the text of such recommendation shall be printed with or annexed to every such bill.
And 79(3) states, and I quote:
When estimates are brought in, the message from the Governor General shall be presented to and read by the Speaker in the House.
Standing Order 80(1) states, and I quote:
All aids and supplies granted to the Sovereign by the Parliament of Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
That is a Standing Order of this House in place since Confederation. Standing Order 80(2) states:
In order to expedite the business of Parliament, the House will not insist on the privilege claimed and exercised by them of laying aside bills sent from the Senate because they impose pecuniary penalties nor of laying aside amendments made by the Senate because they introduce into or alter pecuniary penalties in bills sent to them by this House; provided that all such penalties thereby imposed are only to punish or prevent crimes and offences, and do not tend to lay a burden

Government Orders
on the subject, either as aid or supply to the Sovereign, or for any general or special purposes, by rates, tolls, assessments or otherwise.
In other words, it states absolutely and clearly in the Standing Orders that only this House, not the other place, only this House ,in all questions of supply, namely taking the funds from the Consolidated Revenue Fund has the right to decide how they are to be spent, not the Senate, under any circumstances at any time since Confederation. That is a Standing Order of this House.
That Standing Order does not stand in isolation. Clause 53 of the Constitution Act of Canada states:
Bills for appropriating any Part of the Public Revenue, or for imposing any Thx or Impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
Clause 54 states:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any Vote, Resolution, Address or Bill for the Appropriation of any Part of the Public Revenue, or of any Tax or Impost to any Purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by Message of the Governor General in the Session in which such Vote, Resolution, Address or Bill is proposed.
Nothing could be clearer than that in terms of the constitutional authorities of this House, and solely this House, to deal with tax and spending.
Notwithstanding that, these rights and powers of the Commons vis-a-vis the Senate with respect to legislation and amendments to bills have been seriously and substantially breached by the Senate amendments before us now.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly obvious the Senate has exceeded its role and that on the whole, its amendments alter the very foundation of the government's changes as set forth in Bill C-21. The scope of these amendments and their financial impact on Canadian taxpayers are unacceptable, coming as they do from a group of non-elected senators who are not accountable to anyone for their actions.

It is absolutely incredible in this day and age when everywhere around the world non-elected bodies are being disposed of left, right and centre. In South America elected legislatures and executives are in place where
previously we had non-elected groups. In eastern Europe non-elected parties in power are being thrown out of their various legislatures.
But here in Canada, we have a non-elected group which cannot accept the results of the 1984 election stating that it will not let this elected Chamber do what it was elected to do, namely, deal with the spending and raising funds.
The hon. member-and I await his address with interest-says the Constitution can do it. He says that legally, the Senate can kill a bill. Legally, the monarch can kill a bill. Legally, the Governor General can amend and kill a bill. Legally, the Governor General can do that but never would because the Governor General learned in 1925 that this is a democracy and Governors General do not do that. We need to teach the same lesson to the other place.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: You have no mandate.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I hear talk of mandate. Would the hon. member tell me what mandate the Senate has to do what it has done? What mandate? From whom? What deity bequeaths to these has-been Trudeauites the right to decide the agenda of this country? What deity has prescribed that right to them? They are Liberals? Does that give them a right? The God-given right to say: "To heck with the House of Commons. The House of Commons amounts to nothing. We shall decide in the Senate. We, after all, are appointed by Pierre Elliott Trudeau. This gives us a moral authority beyond mere election in a ballot. This gives us the authority to decide. We may have been tossed out in 1984, but we are still in power, by golly, and we are going to exercise that power". Yes, Sir, only a Liberal could say that without blushing. I will admit the hon. member for Beaches is blushing a little bit.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Broadview-Greenwood. Say it with respect.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Broadview-Greenwood. I am sorry. I am sorry you are not running. You are a lot better than the other bunch that is up there.
I am aware that the other place historically has not accepted the Constitution and our Standing Orders. It continues to claim and has continued to claim in the past that it has some authority.

March 12, 1990

If I may I will quote from a book by Mr. F.A. Kunz entitled The Modem Senate of Canada which deals with the period up to 1963. We have not had any political scientist look at the Senate since then and I can understand why not.
Page 338 of Mr. Kunz's book states:
While the right to refuse or reject is admittedly within the legal powers of the Senate, for the reason that public money cannot be spent or taxes imposed except under the authority of an act of Parliament -
The Senate claims that since it is a part of Parliament, that gives it the legal authority to reject. I would say again, as I said earlier, the Governor General is a part of Parliament as well. The Governor General has that same legal authority but, of course, would never exercise it.
Kunz continues:
-which implies the consent of the Senate, the House of Commons has taken the view that the provision in section 53 of the BNA Act which requires that the entire bill on which the ultimate law is founded must originate in the Commons prohibits the Senate even to amend money bills downward; for if the Senate amends, then the bill passed by the Senate is not the one that originated in the House of Commons. This attitude, which is incorporated in SO 63 -
That is now Standing Order 80.
- of the Rules of the House of Commons, in effect equates the financial powers of the Senate with those of the House of Lords at the time of Confederation, when the Lords were restricted by constitutional conventions but not as yet by the statutory provisions of the Parliament Act. In contrast, the Senate's stand crystallized in the so-called Ross Report of 1918, which served both as a summary of past practice and as a guide for future action, has always been that of the two restrictions on the rights of the House of Lords which the House of Commons by its Resolution of 1678 tried to impose, namely the denial of the right to originate and the denial of the right to amend money bills, the BNA Act adopted the first in Section 53 but did not mention the second and that this proved that the Fathers did not intend the Senate to follow the practice of the House of Lords and not to amend a money bill -
But these arguments and counter-arguments respecting the Senate's financial powers, although theoretically interesting, are now-a-days little more than examples of academic pedantry and to discuss the Senate's right to revise the Government's financial program in terms of conflict is really to present a very misleading picture of its functions in the modern state. On the contrary, the Senate has acted in full understanding of the meaning and implications of responsible government and accepted as binding upon itself the proposition that it should not unduly disturb what has come to be called "the balance of ways and means"; or, as Hopkins says, "that it would be inadmissible to tamper with the overall
Government Orders
financial program submitted by the Government in its budgetary proposals in such a way as to effect a material change in the budgetary surplus or deficit envisaged therein."
This applied to Senators in the other place right up until 1984. What big constitutional changed occurred in 1984? A bunch of Trudeauites got transferred from here over there and they forgot that there was an election which changed where the power should lie. That is all that happened.
In 1963 we have an authority saying that previous Senates have never acted in the way this one is acting. This one has gone back to pre-1678, and they are talking about a modem Senate!
The reality remains that the Commons must, at times such as the present circumstances, reassert its rights to the Senate. It is our responsibility to make such objection. We owe it to the democratic principles upon which the country is based.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The absolute basic grounds on which the Senate must respond to the Commons' will is the fact that this House is elected and the other place is not. That is the foundation of our Canadian democratic system. The reality is in fact understood and accepted by the Senate, we believe.
In recent examples of Senate messages on bills, members will recall that ultimately the Senate acknowledged this truth. The senators proposed their amendments, they got our response, they may have made a second effort to ask us to accept some of their amendments, but, as Senator Frith, the Deputy Leader of the Opposition in the other place, has put it so well, and I believe I quote his words: "There may be 100 reasons why we should not in the Senate yield to the House and only one reason why we should, and if that one reason is that the Commons is elected and the Senate is not then that is reason enough to yield".

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Government is being firm on this principle because it is so absolutely basic to the integrity of our system of responsible government, with a capital R, within a bicameral federal Parliamentary system.

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
The consequences of allowing the Senate to proceed in its course unchallenged, essentially to change the parent Unemployment Insurance Act in sections opened up by Bill C-21, are horrendous implications for democracy and responsible government.
To give one example, in looking at Senate amendments 7 and 9, there is a fundamental deviation from, in fact a wholesale gutting of, one of the principles and the manner of funding which is at the heart of Bill C-21. The effect of implementing these amendments would be an additional expenditure by the government of $1.75 billion above what was planned for in the 1989 budget-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Outrageous.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
-and approved in votes by this House and as reflected in Bill C-21, and its royal recommendation. I urge hon. members to look at page 30, of the April 27, 1989 budget papers, where the finance minister is explicit about UI premiums financing all UI expenditures.
It would be an horrendous thing to imagine that this House would allow the other place to upset budgetary calculations and projections by almost $2 billion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What is democracy anyway?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member from the back row says: "What is democracy anyway". If the Senate speaks, who cares about democratic principles. The hon. member does not care much about democratic principles, obviously, by his bellowing from the back row there.
My point is simply that our Standing Orders and practices, and our Constitution and its history give the Commons the right and duty to set the spending priorities of the government of Canada. That is absolute. It is not, and never has been, the role of an unelected, unresponsible Senate to interfere with or override it.
Yes, the Senate can legally, perhaps, defeat, delay or amend downward a supply appropriation bill. But it never has. Just as the Governor General can legally kill or amend a bill. But the Governor General never has. The Senate can amend, and it has done so, usually with government approval, bills which had a royal recommendation, but never in modern history, if not earlier, in a
fundamental way, with dramatic consequences for what has been called in the Senate, the balance between ways and means. In short, never in defiance of the terms of a royal recommendation, and that is what has been done by the Senate in this case.
I want to focus on the government's position that Bill C-21 is a money bill, with a royal recommendation which appropriates money. The House of Commons must assert in messages to the Senate, when required as in the present case, that the degree of amendment to such bills, by the Senate especially if not just the Commons, must be properly circumscribed. Given the record of Senate practice in the past half century or so and learned commentary on it we must ask ourselves about the extent to which the Senate can alter, in opposition to the House, a government bill, particularly one based on a royal recommendation as Bill C-21 is.
Given the wording of the royal recommendation and the past interpretations by the Speaker of our Standing Orders 79 and 80 which deal with financial procedure, at what point in the specific content of a bill with a royal recommendation does a limit on its ability to be amended become clear, especially any amendment that would, if implemented, redirect the raising or spending of revenue, into or out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund? In other words, what limits, with an eye to impact on the CRF, are there to amendments to a bill like Bill C-21?
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands walking by muttered something about, not if it did not need a royal recommendation in the first place. He seems to be implying that the bill was out of order when brought in in 1921 by having a royal recommendation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He did not say that. Those are your words.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The bill does need a royal recommendation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It doesn't. Your amendment does.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This is a money bill. An amendment to change the amount by $1.75 billion, to introduce a call on a Consolidated Revenue Fund by $1.75 billion does not need a royal recommendation? That is absurd.
March 12, 1990

My remarks are just an overture to what can be expected to be heard from the Minister of Employment and Immigration who will be talking in more substance about the details of the bill when she participates in the debate on a motion I will introduce shortly. But it is clear that what the Senate has proposed dramatically upsets the principles of the bill and dramatically upsets the financial posture brought forward by the Minister of Finance in the budget of April, 1989. It is beyond the purview of the Senate to do that.
I submit that this House is entitled to take exception to the extent to which the unelected Senate has tried to transform the bill sent to it into something fundamentally different. I am aware of the tradition from Westminster cited in Erskine May, Twenty-first Edition, on page 513. He states:
No objection can be taken to a Lords amendment on the ground of
being outside the scope of the bill, or otherwise as to its orderliness-
Then there is the provision-
-except so far as sanction by way of a financial resolution is concerned -
This was not a ways and means bill, but it did have a royal recommendation which limited money put into play by the bill. The appropriation of public revenue "under the circumstances in the manner and for the purposes set out" in the bill. The royal recommendation says that moneys will be appropriated and spent in the manner and for the purposes set out in the bill.
It is clearly out of order for the other place to say that it will spend it in a different manner and for different purposes than those set out in the bill presented to the Senate by this House. That is clearly out of order.
The principles or purposes of Bill C-21, were and are, to end government financing of the unemployment insurance, to restrict entry to and claim upon the program and to use money from the fund to purchase training programs. The Senate has gutted two of these three principles.
I do not create this submission about the Senate role. One of our prime reference works does. It is called, and I referred to it earlier, The Modem Senate of Canada by F. A. Kunz. It reviews specifically the period from 1925 to 1963. He says "The Senate's unique sense of political self restraint"-that was prior to 1963, not post-1984,
Government Orders
obviously-is the result of many factors, including "the self-consciously subordinate position of the Senate in the framework of responsible government, its remoteness from the real centre of political controversy-he means the hustings, the Commons, the ridings-the relatively high average age of its members, the feeling of security engendered by tenure and the intentional laxity of its party organization". He states:
The ruling spirit of the Senate is a spirit of moderation, of fair play, of due independence, of political self-restraint, with a latent determination at the bottom of all discussion and debates not to go beyond a certain limit, not to abuse the constitutional power which resides in the Chamber, giving way even when acquiescence is lacking, and abstaining from pushing the course or objection to the point of obstruction.
That is how this scholar described the Senate from 1925 to 1963. I do not know what words he would use to describe the Senate since 1984.
In his look at "The Senate versus the Executive" he concludes that the elected Commons has pre-eminence. He says: "The Senate as a parliamentary institution has made no articulate attempts to erect a defence for certain economic and social principles in contradistinction with the express wishes of the elected representatives of the people."
I would cite Bills C-27 of 1977 and C-14 of 1978, and the process of Senate disposition of them, as relevant precedents to this situation. The Senate passed them in all stages in one day. These were bills which made very significant changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Imagine, in 1977 and 1978 that august body down the hall passed those bills, in all stages, in one day, bills which made profound and significant changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Now, it does not seem to view that as the way to operate.
What has happened? The mere fact that an election or two happened to intervene is no reason why that same bunch should not stay in power. After all, they are Liberals, are they not? They have been given this authority by the deity to rule and mere elections do not change that. After all, they are members of the Liberal Party of Canada. They do not let mere elections of a bunch of commoners change what is going to happen in this country. That is absurd.

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
Later, Kunz reminds us that the historic interpretation made in the Commons about the weight of Sections 53 and 54 of the Constitution is this:
Public money cannot be spent or taxes imposed except under the authority of an Act of Parliament which implies the consent of the Senate; and the provision in Section 53, which requires that the entire bill on which the ultimate law is founded must originate in the Commons, prohibits the Senate even to amend bills downward; for if the Senate amends, then the bill passed by the Senate is not the one that originated in the House of Commons.
That is axiomatic. All bills which would spend money or raise taxes must originate here. That constitutional provision becomes ludicrous if in fact the other place is able to gut it and say that it will not pass anything but its gutted version. Then what of this authority that the House of Commons possesses by virtue of the Constitution and a few centuries of tradition?
I find it absolutely astounding that for the potential opportunity of short term political gain the opposition parties apparently-I say apparently, we will see what they say in debate; I do not want to pre-judge-are quite willing to dismiss and ignore a few centuries of democratic tradition because there may be an opportunity for some short term political gain.
As I said before, this discussion gets into pedantry because the Senate had not acted so. From 1925 to 1963 the Senate never acted so, and it did not act that way from 1963 to 1984. For 60 years, roughly, we had a Senate that recognized we lived in a democracy. But then the damn democracy went and elected people from the other party. It was an outrageous thing they did, and they did it twice. These protectors of the public in the Senate must prevent the mob in the House of Commons from getting its way.
All that remains is for me to establish that Bill C-21 is in fact a money bill. It is, and I will explain why. Section 53 of the Constitution Act, 1987, provides:
53. Bills for appropriating any Part of the Public Revenue, or for imposing any Ihx or Impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
Bills referred to in Section 53 are commonly referred to as "money bills". That is to say that they deal with what is raised by way of taxes. We know that we need a Ways and Means motion passed by this House before we are able to raise taxes. They deal with what is spent, public revenue. We know that in order to do that we
must have a Royal Recommendation. The Means and Ways role and the supply role both must be established by this House of Commons, preceded in one case by Ways and Means motions and on the outside, if you will, a Royal Recommendation. We cannot raise money without a Ways and Means motion by this House. We cannot spend it without a Royal Recommendation.
It is very clear. This is a prerogative of the House of Commons and only the House of Commons, and not the Senate. To tamper with that in any significant way is clearly and absolutely unacceptable in a democracy.
Again, I can see that legally the Senate may be able to do this. The Government General legally can do that. But in a democracy it is intolerable for either element of Parliament to act against the wishes of a democratically elected House of Commons.
Section 53 prohibits the Senate from amending money bills. In this regard, Standing Order 80 of the House of Commons declares:
80.(1) All aids and supplies granted to the Sovereign by the Parliament of Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, -
Only the House has the right to direct, to limit and to appoint.
- the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
That is from our Standing Orders. It would be in contempt of this House for hon. members to stand up and say that they do not care what Standing Order 80 says, they intend to agree with the Senate's butchering of this Standing Order.
As I have indicated, the term "money bill" refers to a bill that appropriates any part of the public revenue or imposes any tax or impost. Any appropriation, tax or impost is a money bill. In other words, Section 53 applies with respect of any bill that proposes to authorize an expenditure of public money or to impose any tax or impost. In the case of a bill authorizing the expenditure of public money, the authorization may be direct, as in the case of an appropriation bill, or indirect, as in the case of a bill that authorizes or requires something that entails the expenditure of public money.
March 12, 1990

If you see Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure and Practice in the Dominion of Canada, Third Edition, 1903, at page 626, he states:
As a general rule, public bills may originate in either House or whenever; but whenever they grant supplies of any kind, or involve directly or indirectly the levying or appropriation of any tax upon the people, they must be initiated in accordance with law and constitutional practice.
Section 53 of the British North America Act, 1867, expressly provides:
Bills for appropriating any Part of the Public Revenue or for imposing any Thx or Impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
Some instances of bills considered to be money bills are given in Erskine May Parliamentary Practice. I am referring to the 19th edition, page 758, 1976: (a) provisions extending or altering the purposes of a previously authorized expenditure; (b) provisions increasing the amount of a previously authorized expenditure, which is found at page 759; (c) remissions of amounts paid on account of debts, taxes or fees due to the Crown, which is found at page 756; and (d) provisions increasing a charge by the extension of time, found at page 757.
I think that should prove it, but people still argue is Bill C-21 a money bill? One argument that may have been expressed at the Senate or its offices was that since expenditures under the UI Act are paid from a special levy on employers and employees for that purpose and since no general tax revenues were appropriated to pay for these expenditures, there was in effect a separate fund which should not be regarded as public funds or the public revenue.
In response, I say that the UI account is not a separate fund from the CRF. All accounts received under the UI Act on account of premiums are paid into the CRF and all amounts paid as or on account of benefits and assistance under Section 26.1 are paid out of the CRF. I refer members to Sections 113 and 117 of the UI Act.
The CRF is public money or public revenue. In this regard it can be noted that the CRF is defined in Section 2 of the Financial Administration Act as meaning "the aggregate of all public moneys that are on deposit at the credit of the Receiver General". Public money, in turn, is defined as meaning:
Government Orders
All money belonging to Canada received or collected by the Receiver General or any other public officer in his official capacity or any person authorized to receive or collect such money, and includes
(a)	duties and revenue of Canada,
(b)	money borrowed by Canada or received through the issue of sale of securities,
(c)	money received or collected for or on behalf of Canada, and
(d)	all money that is paid to or received or collected by a public officer under or pursuant to any act, trust, treaty, undertaking or contract, and is to be disbursed for a purpose specified in or pursuant to that act, trust, treaty, undertaking or contract.
The point is this. The fact that money raised for UI Act expenditures is raised by a special levy on employers and employees does not mean the moneys are not public moneys or public revenue. There are several provisions in Bill C-21 that have the effect of either directly or indirectly imposing a charge on public funds. These provisions create special new and distinct charges on public funds. These include Clauses 2(1), 9, 14(1), 19(2), 20 and 50(1).
I expect that the Minister of Employment and Immigration will speak to these very important provisions which must be protected when she enters the debate later. The only point I underline now and again is that this money bill has been unacceptably gutted and perverted by some of the Senate amendments.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall what the former Leader of the Opposition said a few years ago, when the Senate tried to force the government to amend the bill to amend the Patent Act. He said at the time:
That the House of Commons should prevail, and that this was the position of the Liberal Party.

Those were the words of the previous leader of this party who stated explicitly in this House that at the end of the day the will of the elected House of Commons must prevail. That is the clear position of the Liberal party. I hope that party with its great democratic tradition will remember those words when it comes to voting on this motion.
Therefore, I move:

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House agrees with amendment 4(A) made by the Senate to Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, but disagrees with amendments 2(A), (B) and (C), 3(A) and (B), 5(A) and (B), 6, 7 and 9 because this House believes that they contradict the principles of the Bill, and violate the traditional legislative role asserted by the Commons in fulfilment of its obligations under Sections 5 3 and 54 of the Constitution Act, as fitting for the unelected Senate on money bills, for the following reasons:
All of them are in contradiction of the fundamental principles contained in C-21, which are:
(I)	a shift to full financing of the UI program though employer and employee premiums;
(II)	a reduction of work disincentives in the UI program;
(III)	an increase in the Government's flexibility to meet the changing needs of UI claimants, to use UI funds to purchase training or provide ancillary income support and to provide access to other active employment measures in accordance with the rights and needs of claimants.

Amendments 2(a), (b) and (c) would restrict the innovative use of U.I. funds for developmental purposes by restricting the Commission's flexibility in purchasing training courses, providing mobility assistance, promoting self-employment and providing claimants with positive work incentives, including bonuses and temporary earnings supplements. This amendment offends principle (iii) mentioned above. It limits the govemments's power to provide active employment measures to claimants.

Amendments 3(A) and (B) would restrict the ability of the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission to design developmental uses benefits and to administer the referral process in ways which are sufficiently flexible to meet the evolving needs of UI claimants, while safeguarding the rights and entitlements otherwise available to UI claimants under the UI Act. Again, this contradicts principle (III).
Amendments 5(A) and (B) would relax the stricter penalties imposed on UI claimants who have quit a job without just cause. This alters principle (II).
Amendment 6 would require that costs associated with third-party training be charged to the new developmental uses portion of the UI account, thereby reducing the funds available to train UI claimants. This contradicts principle (III), as it reduces the government's ability to provide claimants access to active employment measures.
Amendment 7 reinstates Consolidated Revenue Fund responsibility for financing a portion of regional benefits. This contradicts principle (I) of Bill C-21, which requires employee and employer funding of all UI program expenditures.
Amendment 9 would maintain the current programs financing provisions for self-employed fishing benefits. This offends principle (I) above, which ensures that the program must be funded from employer and employee premiums.
And that this House agrees with the principles set out in parts of amendments 1, 4(B), (C) and (D) and 8, but would propose the following amendments:
Amendment 1 be amended to read as follows:

Amendment 4(B) be amended to read as follows:
''Strike out line 4 on page 16 and substitute the following:
Made under Sections 24 to 26.1, and
(III) showing the estimated or, where available, the actual expenditures made under this Act in each province for each of the three years preceding the year to which the plan applies, and"

'Add, immediately after line 6 on page 16, the following:
(2.1) In the Estimates of the expenditures referred to in subparagraphs 2(A)(1) and (II), the plan may include the estimated expenditures to be made in each province".
