That is the motion I put to the House for consideration. I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the end of the day has come and that it is time for the will of the House of Commons to prevail.
Just by way of information to give some indication of how much discussion has gone on so far in this matter, we have previously debated this legislation at second reading for 13 hours. We debated it in committee for 118 hours. We had report stage, we travelled and there were witnesses. We had report stage debate here for seven hours and third reading debate here, for 145 hours in total.
This committee had 233 persons representing 204 groups appear before it. They travelled to Sudbury, Toronto, Jonquiere, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Moncton, and Vancouver, virtually around the entire country.
The Senate has had the bill for some extended months. It also heard many, many witnesses.
I think it is time that the will of the democratically elected people of Canada as expressed by this House of Commons be allowed to prevail and that we move on to other subjects.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be true that there were 13 hours of debate in this House on this bill last fall. We are starting today a debate and we have only had a little more than an hour on a message from the Senate which I think did a terrific job of looking at that bill, as rightly it should. It recommended to this House changes which it has a constitutional right to do. By constitutional obligation it has a right to look at this and give us its opinion. There is nothing wrong with the message we got from the Senate in terms of its constitutional acceptability. I do take exception to the minister wanting us to believe that there
Government Orders
have been 153 hours of debate. That is not what we understand debate to be. There have been 13 hours in this House, and that is about it. I hope he gives us that much time on this message.
First, before addressing the comments and reply of the minister, I would like to remind him that Bill C-21 is an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act. This is not, in our view, a money bill. It reduces the charge on the public treasury rather than being a bill that stands by itself. I will get to the arguments that were put by the department when I get to that question of whether indeed this is a money bill, yes or no.
I want to make a couple of comments before I get into the meat of the matter. We must remember that Canada, unlike the United Kingdom, is a federation. We do not have a unicameral parliament. We have the House of Commons that proposes and we have the Senate that can propose in certain circumstances.
In 1867 there were those in this country who opposed the establishment of the Senate. They wanted a Parliament constituted strictly on the basis of representation by population. Those persons, we will recall, were mostly from Canada west, which is now Ontario, my province. They did not prevail. They did not win their argument. The other provinces refused to agree to a Parliament in which one province, in this case Ontario, was expected to be dominant.
Those of us who come from Central Canada, as it is called, either Ontario or Quebec, must recognize, however, that members of the House of Commons are elected and have a most important role to perform, namely, to represent the people of the other provinces against a central majority dominated House of Commons. It is quite possible, and we have heard some arguments today, that an elected Senate could be far more effective than the present one. We are not debating that here today. I, for one, believe that an elected Senate would be more effective. However, until we do have an elected Senate, the Senate as now constituted must perform the tasks assigned to it by our Constitution.
I come directly to the question. Are the amendments before this House put by the Senate of Canada unacceptable to this House, either because they contravene our Standing Orders, as was alluded to by the minister, that

Government Orders
is, Standing Order 80(1), or because they contravene Sections 53 or 54 of the Constitution Act, 1867?
I could not find anybody in the Senate who said: "We accepted Standing Order 80(1) of this House". That Standing Order is quite clear. Standing Order 80(1) states:
All aids and supplies granted to the Sovereign by the Parliament of
Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for
granting such aids and supplies-
I underline the words "aids and supplies" because that is very important to my argument.
- ought to begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
The question we have to answer is whether Bill C-21 deals with aids and supplies such as described in Standing Order 80(1). In my opinion clearly it does not. We need not to revive the old argument between the House of Commons and the Senate, the dispute over whether Standing Order 80(1) prevails.
If we go into the authorities and look at Erskine May, Erskine May says: "Charges upon the public revenue are of two kinds." I think it is important that people understand that there are two kinds of charges against the public revenue: charges payable out of money to be provided by Parliament, that is, moneys to be voted year by year. That is the ways and means motions and supply motion under which we operate every year. That is one way.
Then there are charges upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund as a second source of supply. The charges payable out of the money to be provided by Parliament under the moneys that are voted every year are authorized every year by the regular appropriation acts of this House. The charges upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund are called statutory expenditures. That is what Bill C-21 addresses. It is not the aids and supplies argument but the statutory expenditures.
Historically, the Crown was expected to pay the annual costs of the Public Service from the income from Crown
lands and the like. When this proved inadequate the Crown turned to Parliament for aids and supplies, that is, for financial supplements to make up the total requirements for each year. It is to the regular appropriation bills that Standing Order 80(1) refers.
At Westminster the bills granting aids and supplies are presented by Royal Assent by the Speaker of the House of Commons. The same thing happens here in Canada. A bill must have a royal recommendation to be called a statutory expenditure. Once we clear that up we must address the other kinds of charges I just alluded to as statutory expenditures.
They do not begin with a request for supply, nor are they dealt with according to the Standing Orders of the Business of Supply. Before 1968 they began with financial resolutions moved in a committee of the whole House. The terms of such resolutions were recommended to the House by the Governor General and in 1968 the preliminary resolution stage was dropped in Canada. Since then, the royal recommendation is communicated to the House in the manner prescribed in Standing Order 79(2).
Bill C-21 was introduced with a royal recommendation as prescribed by Standing Order 79(2), not with a royal recommendation presented in the manner prescribed by Standing Order 79(3). I think it would be of some assistance if I read Standing Orders 79(2) and 79(3):
(2)	The message and recommendation of the Governor General in relation to any bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or of any tax or impost shall be printed on the Notice Paper and in the Votes and Proceedings when any such measure is to be introduced and the text of such recommendation shall be printed with or annexed to every such bill.
(3)	When estimates are brought in, the message from the Governor General shall be presented to and read by the Speaker in the House.
I think one must accept that Bill C-21 is not a bill supplying aids and supplies. Standing Order 81 does not apply to it, but Standing Orders 79(2) and 79(3) apply.
Having said that we have to address the constitutional question. Are these amendments put by the Senate out of order because of Section 54 of the 1867 Constitution Act? Bill C-21 is a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970, 1971 and 1972.
March 12, 1990

I remind members that the original bill was Bill C-229. It became the Unemployment Insurance Act. It was read the first time on March 10, 1971. That is the original bill which this Bill C-21 wants to amend. The appropriation sought by the bill was recommended by the Governor General and there was an appropriate royal recommendation.
If we look at the clauses of Bill C-21 which the Senate proposes to amend, every one of those clauses could have been moved in 1971 as an amendment to Bill C-229 by any private member of this House. None of those clauses of Bill C-21 seeks to increase the amount or to change the purpose of an appropriation in any way in conflict with the royal recommendation of March 10, 1971.
It follows that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-21 do not offend that recommendation. If Bill C-229 adopted by this House on March 10,1971 were in order, we believe the Senate amendments before this House today, in 1990, which in no case go beyond the appropriation made by the bill originally are in order. Given the fact that all the provisions of Bill C-21 could have been moved in 1971 as amendments to the original Bill C-229, one must ask why Bill C-21 was introduced in this House with a royal recommendation. Bill C-21 was introduced into the House on June 1, 1989 and the royal recommendation attached to it read:
Her Excellency the Governor General recommends to the House of Commons the appropriation of public revenue under the circumstances, in the manner and for the purposes set out in the measure entitled An Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act.
When the officials were questioned in committee on February 5, 1990 as to which clauses of Bill C-21 in their opinion required a royal recommendation-in other words, why Bill C-21 which is an amendment to the original bill required a royal recommendation-their reply was that no analysis had been made by either the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission or the Department of Justice to ascertain which of those clauses did indeed require a royal recommendation. If any clause required it, we did not find out. They did not know. If none of the clauses amended by the Senate require a royal recommendation in our view, it follows that in so far as those clauses are concerned the royal
Government Orders
recommendation of June 1, 1989 is irrelevant. That was the basis of the argument in the Senate.
The Speaker of the Senate found the arguments so convincing that he ruled squarely on Erskine May. He found that indeed the amendments were in order and that they did not impose an extra charge on the public treasury, that Bill C-21 was not a money bill but indeed reduced the charges on the public treasury and therefore was acceptable.

Mr. Speaker, I would now like to talk about the amendments or rather the amendment that the government has accepted, Amendment 4(a), and a few more that they accepted with amendments at the same time that they rejected very important amendments which we thought would restore some fairness for Canadian workers in terms of their rights, as we see them, to unemployment insurance benefits.
I would like to talk about the nine amendments proposed by the Senate which we think greatly improve Bill C-21. We do not claim that these proposals are excellent. There is no pretention of excellence but we claimed, Mr. Speaker, that it was possible to improve the bill and it was in that spirit that the Senate made these nine amendments.
As I was saying, the Conservative government, through its minister, showed its intention to make very complex changes to three of these amendments: training, including literacy, the department's plan for regional benefits and fishermen's benefits.
Mr. Speaker, during the debate, Liberal members will elaborate on these amendments and give arguments for broadening them, we hope.
Amendment No. 5 on penalties and Amendment No. 7 on the government's withdrawal from UI funding were rejected by the government. The government intends to oppose Amendment No. 2 on training, the "Henry VIII" clause, Amendment No. 3, Amendment No. 6, privatization, and No. 9, benefits taken over by the government.
For the Senate, Mr. Speaker, these nine amendments are an acceptable compromise on a bill which has many flaws. I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, that most of those who spoke in committee and in this House tried

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
very hard to make the government understand the problems with this bill.
I shall explain to you, Mr. Speaker, not in numerical order but in my order of priority, the reasons for each of the amendments made by the Senate.
Concerning the government's withdrawal from the unemployment insurance program, Amendment No. 7, many witnesses who appeared before the committee on Bill C-21 were unanimous in saying that this measure was the most significant of all the proposed changes. Therefore, concerned about the considerable problems which this change might cause, the members of the Senate Committee have proposed Amendment No. 7 to keep section 118 in the Unemployment Insurance Act so that the government would have to fund not all but half the cost of extended regional benefits from general revenues and not the UI account.
Mr. Speaker, we believe that one of the reasons why the government withdrew from funding the program was the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. When it signed the agreement, the government either did not think, or simply preferred not to tell Canadians, that the United States might consider the unemployment insurance program as a kind of hidden subsidy. To observe its part of the agreement with our American neighbours, the Conservative government had no hesitation in withdrawing completely from the program's financing. To harmonize-that is the term being used-its operations with the United States, this government did not think twice about putting the whole financial burden on Canadian workers and by the same token, had no hesitation in shirking its social and economic responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, I would urge hon. members to read the latest issue of the magazine Relations. It contains an article on Bill C-21 by Henri Sader, "Le salaire de la peur". I won't have time to read it to you, but I strongly urge hon. members to read it. I think this article is very worthwhile, and if I had time, I would quote from it at length to make my case. However, I think all hon. members received this publication at their offices. I advise them to read it.
In 1971, the federal government started funding regional extended benefits, the extended benefits paid under section 25, job creation, and section 26, training, as
well as net benefits paid to independent fishermen. More specifically, the government started financing benefits to cover the difference between the real unemployment rate and a rate of 4 per cent. Under Bill C-21, the Unemployment Insurance Fund will pay benefits only when the unemployment rate rises above 6 per cent. The government will no longer finance extended benefits based on the regional unemployment rate, fishermen's benefits or its share of manpower programs. In the United States, Mr. Speaker, this bill would make Canada the only industrialized country with a system to which its government did not contribute a cent.
Bill C-21 repeals section 118 of the Act, which concerns government contributions to extended benefits, and also subsection 130(3) which concerns government contributions to net benefits paid to independent fishermen. This change, I think, is a sign that the government is not intent on improving the unemployment insurance system but on harmonizing with our American neighbours while trying to cope with the deficit.
In fact, what this Government has done is save $2.2 billion at the expense of employees who see their unemployment insurance premiums increase from $1.95 to $2.25 on each $100 earned and at the expense of the employers whose share is or will be 1.4 times that of their employees.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to remind the hon. members that, on November 8, 1984, the then Minister of Employment and Immigration, Miss MacDonald, stated, and I quote:
Any substantial increase of the premium rate would bring about
additional costs which would be difficult to bear for the businesses
and which would hinder job creation in the private sector.
Mr. Speaker, that leading Conservative cabinet minister was speaking for the government in those days.
In my riding, Ottawa University will be one of the first to be hard hit by such measure.
Indeed, Ottawa university will be forced to seriously review its budget for it will have to pay $400,000 more into the Unemployment Insurance Fund. Mr. Speaker, this may be peanuts for a multinational but, for a university operating on already limited budgets, additional expenditures of the sort have a devastating effect on the progress of an institution already hardly hit by
March 12, 1990

other measures as negative as the one imposed by this government.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote also a comment from the Ontario Coalition for Social Justice. Laurell Ritchie said and I quote: "One can raisonnably expect that, by 1993, when much bigger premiums will be necessary to sustain the Fund, the employers who are now contributing the largest share to the Plan will have managed to ask first of all for new reductions."
Another important argument was raised by Mitchell Kosney of the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto, and I quote: "This bill removes a major and significant impetus for the government's commitment to full employment policies and on the unemployed and economically depressed regions and workers caught in the growing and ever-increasing number of poor quality, low-paid jobs."
Let us now deal with Amendment No. 8:

Let us deal with the fishermen's benefits amendment. The Senate committee also brought forth three amendments relating to fishermen's benefits. In 1956 the Unemployment Insurance Act was amended to extend coverage to self-employed fishermen. Section 130 of the Unemployment Insurance Act provides that the Unemployment Insurance Commission may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, make such regulations as it deems necessary to establish and operate a scheme of unemployment insurance for self-employed persons engaged in fishing or activities incidental to fishing.
Fishermen's unemployment insurance premiums go into the Consolidated Revenue Fund and benefits are paid from that fund. The government therefore finances from general revenue the difference between the benefits paid and the premiums collected from self-employed fishermen. That is the government's contribution and in 1988 it amounted to $248 million. Some 35,000 fishermen benefited from this program.
By repealing Section 130(3) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, clause 53 of Bill C-21 ends all direct government financing. Fishermen's benefits would in the future be paid from the unemployment insurance account which will funded solely by premiums. The effect is to withdraw government funding of fishermen's benefits and to ensure that expenditure for these benefits is
Government Orders
treated on the same basis as expenditure for any other benefit.
There are dangers to the elimination of the status of self-employed fishermen and to cutting back the payments that they will receive. Since the unemployment insurance account would now be responsible for all fishermen's benefits, pressure could be expected to develop from other premium contributors to reduce these benefits and even possibly to eliminate the special status of self-employed fishermen under the act.
In 1988, fishermen paid approximately $18 million into the fund and received roughly $269 million in benefits. The government, therefore, made up the difference from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of some $251 million.
Mr. Earl McCurdy from the Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers Union stated:
Business groups will be fighting tooth and nail in the years to come
to take the position that, since the government is out, they regard
themselves as having to subsidize fishermen's unemployment
insurance-and they will say "that is not fair and we want out."
Therefore, the Senate is asking the government to continue to finance benefit payments in excess of premiums collected. We believe that would be justified.
The second part of the amendment proposed by the Senate would also have the effect of reducing the vulnerability of fishermen's benefits by making any change to the regulations dealing with self-employed fishermen, subject to the approval of Parliament.
At the present time regulations concerning fishermen's benefits can be changed without Parliament's approval. Unemployment insurance benefits to fishermen could be revoked by the approval of the Governor in Council only.
The amendment proposed by the Senate provides that to stop a motion which proposes to modify the regulations concerning fishermen's benefits, the signature of no fewer than 15 senators or 30 members of this House of Commons would be required.
Members of this House will remember that a similar clause was inserted in Section 87 of the Official Languages Act. We did that a year and a half ago. It was good then. Why can we not do that today? For regulations can be changed at any time by Order in Council, why not have public scrutiny? Why not have this transparence in regard to a program of such importance? We have it in the Official Languages Act. We think it would be a good

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
idea to have it in regard to regulations affecting fishermen.
The final part of the Senate amendment will repeal subsection 130(4) of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Subsection 130(4) provides that the whole section dealing with fishermen's benefits may be repealed by the government by simple proclamation. That subsection, originally introduced in the 1971 Unemployment Insurance Act, was intended to record the transitional nature of Section 130 of the act until:
-the plans being developed to protect self-employed fishermen against the uncertainties inherent in the primary fishing industry are ready for implementation.
That is from the White Paper on Unemployment Insurance in 1970, page 11.
Indeed to give the cabinet that power to revoke or to change the regulations without consultation with Parliament was supposed to be an interim measure. However the fishermen's special status, well deserved by the way, remained largely unchanged and still today is transitional. The proposed amendment to the act would make it permanent and would eliminate the uncertainties inherent in this act. To this effect the Senate committee report says:
Your committee believes that in view of the crisis in the Atlantic fisheries, concrete steps should be taken to protect the benefits now provided to self-employed fishermen and to provide assurance that the government is in fact committed to the maintenance of this vital program.

Mr. Speaker, in 1977, the Unemployment Insurance Plan adopted a variable entrance requirement which tied the number of insurable weeks of employment required for benefits to the unemployment rate. To be eligible, those who lived in a region where the unemployment rate was less than or equal to 6 per cent had to have at least 14 weeks of insurable employment. In all regions where the unemployment rate was greater than 9 per cent, a minimum of 10 weeks of work was required. Every year, the government presented legislation which was adopted by Parliament to extend the variable entrance requirements. In 1989, the Conservative government refused to continue with this formula, Mr. Speaker; it refused in the House to extend this variable entrance requirement for Canadian workers. The Conservatives refuse to pass this legislation, thereby penalizing thousands of jobless Canadians.
The Conservative government has contemptuous attitude towards unemployed Canadians. The Conservative government had a choice between maintaining the present support for the unemployed and adopting an attitude of confrontation with the Senate.
And good God, Mr. Speaker, with the minister's statement today, we know what decision they have made. They decided to go for a confrontation with the Senate.
The Prime Minister chose to abandon the unemployed, proving once again his indiferrence to the less fortunate in our society. If the Prime Minister were in good faith, Mr. Speaker, he would have allowed the bill extending the variable entrance requirement to pass as was proposed in the House not veiy long ago, in January.
Passing Senate Bill S-12 would have enabled workers who lost their job to still be eligible for the existing unemployment insurance benefits after January 6, 1990.
Mr. Speaker, we deplored it at the time and we still deplore the government's attitude to Canada's unemployed.
Bill C-21 proposes to introduce a modified version of the variable entrance requirement. Instead of 10 to 14 weeks, 10 to 20 weeks of insurable employment would be required. All regions with unemployment rates of 6 per cent or less would require as many as 20 weeks of insurable employment, while only those regions with an unemployment rate of more than 15 per cent would retain a minimum entrance requirement of 10 weeks.
Bill C-21 proposes a new, 62-region system. Under this system and the new entrance requirements, according to the report of the Special Committee of the Senate on Bill C-21, claimants in 45 regions would require more than 14 weeks of insurable earnings, while the minimum 10-week entrance requirement would apply only in 8 regions.
March 12, 1990

However, under the old variable entrance requirement rules, the minimum would have applied in 32 of these regions. Of the 13 regions in Atlantic Canada, only 5 would qualify at 10 weeks, under Bill C-21, as compared to 12 regions under the old rules. That is more than twice as much, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-21 also changes the benefit structure. In most cases, the proposed change will reduce the maximum duration of benefit entitlement. For instance, according to the information given in the Senate report, claimants in central Nova Scotia, Sherbrooke, Hull right next door, St.Catharines, Sudbury, northern Ontario, southern Manitoba, and Regina would lose up to 13 weeks of benefits. More than 3 months of benefits would be lost by workers who are seeking employment.
Mr. Speaker, claimants in Halifax, Calgary and Vancouver would lose up to 12 weeks of benefits. Workers in St. John's, Newfoundland, Saint John, New Brunswick, Fredericton, Moncton, Quebec City, Trois-Rivieres, Montreal, Chicoutimi, Ottawa, Windsor, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Victoria and Vancouver Island would all lose up to 11 weeks of benefits.
Surprisingly, claimants in regions with an unemployment rate of up to 12 per cent would lose up to 11 weeks, while regions with an unemployment rate under 4 per cent would lose only 3 weeks. It is difficult to reconcile this outcome with the professed objective of Bill C-21, which according to the government, and I quote:
-was designed to ensure that there would no impact in areas where there was high unemployment.
I was quoting Mr. Barry Carin, Assistant Deputy Minister, Employment and Immigration, from his testimony on February 1, 1990, before the Senate Committee.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, the amendments to entrance requirements and benefit duration provided under Bill C-21 will have a very definite impact on many of the regions I just mentioned.

Bill C-21 will hurt the unemployed in just about every region of the country. The federal government, in the document Success in the Works presents some estimates of the impact of these new measures. In Table 13 in that report, on page 25, we see that the age group hardest hit
Government Orders
by Bill C-21 is 25 to 34, absorbing a $450 million reduction in benefits or 38 per cent of the cuts. Table 15, at page 27, shows that 530,000 unemployed Canadians would be affected by the new bill to a total sum of $800 million. The government calls this "savings". This is the biggest attack on the backs of the least fortunate of our society.
Let me remind you of what the Prime Minister said in the last general election. I want to quote because this is very important. In The Sunday Star of October 16, 1988, he said:
As long as I am Prime Minister, social benefits will be improved,
not diminished, by this government.
So much for that. Now this same government is saying to Canadians that it will save $800 million on the backs of these 530,000 Canadians who would be affected by this legislation.
We must keep in mind that these government numbers are based on assumptions. What I have just quoted I have taken from the government's own books. We must keep in mind that they are based on assumptions which will affect Canadians more onerously than anticipated. We can certainly question these figures of the government. That is the role of the opposition.
I just want to quote the firm Global Economics which was commissioned by the Liberal Party of Canada to examine the proposed changes. The conclusions of this study differ significantly from the government's study.
Whereas the government predicts a $1.2 billion decrease in unemployment benefits-$800 million in benefits lost plus $450 million in penalties-the Global Economics study forecasts a drop of $1.5 billion, that 775,000 Canadians will lose benefits with an average loss of $1,486. This loss of benefits is most pronounced in Newfoundland, with an average loss of $2,429; Prince Edward Island with a loss of $2,373 and New Brunswick with a loss of $2,011. Atlantic Canada and Quebec will be the hardest hit. Quebec will lose $507 million as a result of this bill. Nationwide, 80 per cent of the net losers will be earning less than $25,000.
The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives also produced a study which yielded results much closer to those of Global Economics' than those of the government. This study concludes that the decrease in benefits

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
will amount of $1.8 billion, as opposed to $1.2 billion predicted by the government.
The regional impact on the Atlantic provinces will be much worse than the government predicts. The provinces are pessimistic about the effects of C-21. In Newfoundland, according to the provincial study, 19,000 people may not meet the new strict entrance requirements. The Minister of Employment and Labour Relations, Ms. Patricia Cowan is quoted as saying:
Bill C-21 is probably the most devastating thing to come our way in Newfoundland and Labrador, for a long time.
Without immediate attention, this bill will condemn not hundreds, but thousands of Newfoundland families to uncertain futures where poverty and welfare will be commonplace.
Since the last general election, the Conservative Government has slashed regional development to the Atlantic provinces, has dismantled VIA Rail, has done nothing about the crisis in the fisheries and has pushed, with all steam ahead, on Bill C-21, regardless of the consequences.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21 provides for a major transfer of funds from the Unemployment Insurance Fund to training programs. This is one of the major objectives of Bill C-21, which provides that eveiy year, the minister will table in Parliament a plan explaining where the funds will be spent.
The question is, and it is a very important one, where the funds earmarked for training programs will be spent. This question is particularly important since there is no provision in this respect in Bill C-21. No one knows where the funds will be allocated.
What happens if Nova Scotia loses $40 million in benefits when Bill C-21 is passed? Will the province recover those funds in the form of training programs? Will Quebec recover $507 million in lost benefits? Noboby knows. The Minister of Employment and Immigration is unable to answer these questions. The deputy minister said in committee that he did not expect any radical changes in the distribution of funds. The government does not seem to know one way or another and is not prepared to provide the necessary explanations.
The Senate committee proposes an amendment to provide more information on the transfer of funds from the Unemployment Insurance Fund to training programs. Amendment No. 4, which was partially accepted by the government, would make it possible to control distribution of funds, to determine how losses and compensation are shared among the regions. To simplify comparisons between previous expenditures and proposed expenditures, the Senate committee recommends that the plan should indicate expenditures for each of the three years preceding those to which the plan applies. That seems to make sense and it is not terribly complex.
Bill C-21 just says that the plan would have to be approved by the Governor in Council and there is no guarantee that parliamentarians could speak on the planned expenditures and the allocations of funds in the affected regions. The legislation should include a provision that parliamentarians could not only consider the plan but also approve it, Mr. Speaker.
Amendment No. 1, which the government has accepted in principle, concerns literacy training. Mr. Speaker, illiteracy, poverty and unemployment are closely related. Recent estimates show that one Canadian in four is totally or functionally illiterate. Nicole Boily of the Canadian Institute for Adult Education told the Senate Committee:
(The problem you raised of) young people who drop out of school and who are doomed to short-term, unskilled jobs without any security (is a very real one throughout Canada). -We cannot neglect those who already find themselves in this difficult situation.
Still quoting:
I think it is very important that we provide basic education for young people.
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a strong negative correlation between education and unemployment. I want to quote Tracy Westell of the Ontario Literacy Coalition who said recently:
-there is a clear connection between lack of education and unemployment. In the regions in Canada where unemployment is high, the rate of illiteracy is also very high.
Mr. Speaker, according to Bill C-21, unemployed people who receive UI benefits will not be eligible for literacy courses; if they took such courses, they would lose all their benefits. This defies all logic. How can the workers of tomorrow face the technological challenges
March 12, 1990

of tomorrow if they cannot acquire the most basic knowledge?
I think that the government, by saying that it supports the principle, is changing Bill C-21 a little and we will see what happens in the coming days, Mr. Speaker, so that we can comment further on this change.
Senate amendment No. 1 would allow workers entitled to unemployment insurance to enrol in basic training courses, including elementary level proficiency courses, while remaining eligible for benefits. They propose that Bill C-21 lines 37 to 40 be striken out and replaced by the following, and I quote, Mr. Speaker:
For greater certainty, the words "course or program of instruction
or training* in subsection (1) include a course or program of
instruction or training in basic skills or literacy.
Again, Mr. Speaker, to me this seems logical and essential.
I now go on to amendment No. 5. Some of the Unemployment Insurance Act provisions prescribe that a claimant is disentitled for a given period of time for refusing suitable employment or quitting the job without valid reasons.
Under the existing statute a claimant may be disentitled to benefits for a maximum of six weeks. Bill C-21 provides for a much stiffer penalty, ranging from a minimum of seven weeks to a maximum of 12 weeks, double the current maximum.
Mr. Speaker, there is no minimum under the existing law. In addition the proposed legislation would authorize the UI Commission to reduce the rate of benefits to 50 per cent of insurable earnings, down from 60 per cent now. Finally, any part of the disqualification period which has not been served might be deferred for six years.
According to the government figures the new provisions would make it possible to save-Mr. Speaker, I imagine that means "saving" for the government-$450 million whereas 250,000 unemployed workers will lose a minimum of seven weeks of benefits. How can the government justify such drastic treatment of the unemployed? How can the government justify forcing an unemployed worker to wait for up to three months- twelve weeks-before drawing his UI benefits?
Government Orders
Doesn't the Minister know that the big losers in her reform are poor, that 80 per cent of them earn less than $25,000?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Shame!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Three months without pay can be very difficult when one does not have any savings, Mr. Speaker. Isn't it a little too long?
Maybe the minister can live for three months without any income coming in but the unemployed Canadians she proposes to penalize unfairly cannot afford it. That is why we hope the government will change its mind and accept the Senate amendment.
Harassed workers will be afraid to quit their jobs. Harassed workers who know they will lose everything if they quit their jobs or look for employment elsewhere will certainly hesitate and even suffer from fear of losing all benefits and other forms of income for themselves and their families for three months. We find such a severe penalty on families earning less than $25,000 unfair and almost inhuman.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment proposed by the Senate would set the maximum disqualification period at six weeks and the period for carrying forward any portion of a disqualification not served at two years instead of six.
We know it is not perfect but we think it is reasonable since there is no definition of just cause in the legislation to determine whether workers have valid reasons for leaving. Moreover, the disqualification period is two weeks on average in the case of a resignation.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to talk about Amendment No. 2, allocations of funds from the Unemployment Insurance Fund to training. Although we approve of the idea of offering workers some form of occupational training to increase their capacity to earn a living, we nonetheless find absurd that the government would have to draw from the Fund in order to finance training. We suggest that the govemement should not finance training programs by cutting Unemployment Insurance benefits.
As Mrs. Helene Chauvigne, from Mouvement Action-Chomage de I'Outaouais quebecois, pointed out when appearing before the Committee: "Nothing assures us that the people whose UI benefits will be reduced are

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
going to benefit from the training they will be paying for".
To quote another witness, Mrs. Shirley Carr, president of the Canadian Labour Congress: "If the Bill is adopted, we believe, and we have grounds to believe, that the $2 billion in UI premiums which would be redirected to training programs will be used for a large part to replace the Canadian Jobs Strategy. Worse still, that money could be used to finance the relocation of the unemployed, the wage subsidies for businesses and other programs that will be of no help to the unemployed or to the communities".
Mr. Speaker, the first objective of the unemployment insurance plan is to provide income support to workers temporarily out of a job. To use the funds of the plan to buy "training courses" or to strart a business is, in our opinion, contrary to the first objective of the plan. In all fairness, these initiatives should be financed by general revenues, that is to say out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
That is the reason why the Senate committee proposes to strike out lines 13 and 14, as well as lines 38 to 45 on page 14 of Bill C-21. To strike out line 8 and substitute "graph (l)(b) may provide that" on page 15. Amendment No. 2 would prevent the allocation of moneys from the unemployment insurance fund to training.
Furthermore, the fact that the government is prepared to give up to $15,000 to people willing to relocate in areas where unemployment in lower is evidence of the importance, for the government, of "relocation" of people out of regions which are less developed or where industry is cyclical. This approach in Bill C-21 would lead to depopulation of the regions most affected by unemployment. What the gouvernment is proposing is exile from underdeveloped areas.
What is even more troubling, if we follow the rationale of the government, is that claimants would be financing their own moving with the savings realized by cutting benefits. That is why the Senate is opposed to this clause and proposes to strike out lines 34 and 35, on page 14, and substitute the following: "tunities for employment are greater, or moving to".
Mr. Speaker, the Senate Committee also found unacceptable that in Bill C-21 the normal appeal procedure should not apply to the administrative decisions governing the new training methods. We felt that this provision could prove detrimental to the victims of discrimination and minorities. To grant a right to appeal decisions made on the basis of these provisions would be to respect the principles of justice and fairness normally accepted in this country. Therefore, lines 44 and 45, on page 14, as well as lines 1 and 2, on page 15 of Bill C-21 should be struck out.
Mr. Speaker, I come now to amendment No 3, the so-called "Henry VUI" clause. If the Government intends to adopt a policy requiring the unemployed to finance their training programs, it should make sure that the regulations are consistent with the essential provisions of the legislation in this area. We suggest that granting of such discretionary powers on a fund approaching $2 billion is unjustified. The provisions respecting the establishment and operation of the assistance scheme described in Paragraph 26.1(C) are an important component of Bill C-21. They represent the main benefit for which the unemployed would foot the bill following the very significant cuts in their benefits. Yet, the unemployed could not rely on the new schemes offered because under clause 26.1(3), the Unemployment Insurance Commission would have full authority as far as the detailed definition of these schemes is concerned.
This paragraph states that "any scheme established under subsection (1) may, with respect to any matter, be different from the provisions of this Act relating to that matter". If it is called the Henry VIII amendment, it is because there is nothing in this bill which makes it possible for the administration to legislate when there is no provision authorizing it.
As was mentioned by Nicole Boily, from the Canadian Institute of Adult Education, "this paragraph opens the door to infinite possibilities the limits of which would come apparently from the fund's budget".
So, amendment 3 would strike out lines 1 to 6, page 15, of Bill C-21.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to talk about amendment 6 as it relates to the contracting out and privatization of certain activities.
Bill C-21 would give the Commission the power to delegate to third parties certain tasks under the Unem-
March 12, 1990

Government Orders
ployment Insurance Plan. According to clause 49 of the Bill, any amount payable by the Commission for such services would be considered implementation costs, not subject to the 15 per cent limit applicable to training courses. Inevitably, this would further reduce the Unemployment Insurance Fund moneys used to guarantee income security for the unemployed and constitute a further step towards privatization.
While denying that the privatization of UI is a priority, the government is privatizing it by the back door. Moreover, after imposing a 15 per cent limit on expenses other than income security benefits, why would the government create a loophole through which one could circumnent its own policy? Currently, payments to third parties come from the Labour Force Development Strategy. With Bill C-21, these expenses would be paid for by the Unemployment Insurance Plan.
The Senate Committee recommends to strike out lines 37 to 43, page 31, and lines 1 to 6, page 32. Amendment no. 6 would not prevent the making of agreements with third parties but would insure that expenses incurred under such an agreement would be paid for by the unemployment insurance account reserved for expenses not related to income security.

In conclusion, we have heard from many groups and organizations. Today the Liberal caucus heard the joint statement of the labour coalition of unions on Bill C-21. I recommend this reading to all members of the House. I think it is a very interesting position.
I was hoping a government member would ask me to read that, but since they do not insist on me reading it, I possibly could table it for their edification. I could have it printed as an appendix to Hansard, if they will give unanimous consent.
As my friend says, those who can read may want to read this document. It is a very interesting one, put out by the coalition on Bill C-21. If you insist, Mr. Speaker, I could read it into the record. I will leave it to a member of my caucus to do that and to comment positively on it some other day. I am sure there will be unanimous consent for us to recognize the importance of the contribution that the unions play in opposing Bill C-21.
Although many groups, organizations and Canadians from every section of Canada, have maintained that Bill C-21 should not be adopted, the Senate has proposed those amendments which the government should take into consideration and accept for the benefit of all those who would be affected by the proposed legislation.
These amendments brought forward by the Senate would assure a continuation of government contributions to the Unemployment Insurance account and recognition of the federal government's responsibility for regional unemployment. They would also ensure that self-employed fishermen are given continuous protection under the Unemployment Insurance program, and that claimants residing in high unemployment regions are granted better income protection.
By way of these amendments, Liberal Senators sought to reaffirm the principle that unemployment insurance should be used for income maintenance and not for training courses and financing entrepreneurial activities which should be provided in our view, by the government.
I want to thank the Senate for its very important contributions. We will participate in this debate in the hope and with the wish that the government will see the light, will find its way to accepting all of the amendments. To that effect, I move, seconded by the member for Kingston and the Islands:
That the motion be amended by
(1)	deleting the words "amendment 4(a)" in the first paragraph and substituting the words "amendments 1,2A, 2B, 2C, 3A, 3B, 4A, 4B, 4C, 4D, 5A, 5B, 6, 7, 8, and 9" therefor; and by
(2)	deleting all the words after the words "Commission Act" in the first paragraph.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get into the main body of my speech, I cannot help but comment on the choice of words of the minister when he introduced the motion and the way he referred to the Senate and what he perceived the Senate as having done to Bill C-21. He referred to gutting and violating. It is no surprise to me that those are words he

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
would choose after having gutted the Unemployment Insurance Act and violated the Canadian public.
In my speech after the introduction of this bill, I referred to the Dalton gang of Barbara, Michael and Brian riding into town to loot the UIC vault. Now it appears that they are having a shoot-out with the Liberal Senate and unemployed Canadians across the country are running to get out of the cross-fire.
The government response to the Senate does nothing to respond to the serious concerns of people across this country who appeared before the House committee. They told the government that blaming the unemployed for unemployment just is not acceptable. They told the government that they had believed the government when it promised during the last election campaign that it would not touch unemployment insurance. They felt betrayed and that they had no recourse but to look beyond the House of Commons for assistance.
It is not surprising then that the government finds itself in this position. It did not listen to the groups that told it of the devastating and harmful impact of Bill C-21. It did not listen to recommendations of an all-party committee, after the Forget Commission, nor did it listen to the minority report to the Forget Commission itself. The government did not even listen to the minister's own advisory committee which, in report after report, recommended enhancing the UI system, not destroying it. That this government does not listen will be no surprise. It should also come as no great surprise that the Liberals do not listen very well either.
Granted in this package of amendments we do find some things which could be supported, such as allowing people to collect UI during basic literacy training. That is something the New Democratic Party has supported all along. Extended benefits for fisheries during this time of crisis is also something we could support. But these amendments, taken as a whole, still represent a fundamental cut to benefits and support for the unemployed.
The government is tinkering, it is putting sugar coating on a poison bill, to quote the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. Therefore, we cannot support it.
Had the Liberals really wanted to offer an alternative to Canadians, they had the opportunity. Hundreds of
groups appeared from across the country and offered good and solid advice. The Liberals have never been friends of unemployment insurance and during their mandate ushered in cuts to benefits and significant withdrawal of federal money from the program.
Let us review some of the Liberal record. In 1976, the Liberals reduced the maximum coverage from 75 years of age to 65. The Liberals also reduced the benefit rate for claimants with families from 75 per cent of insurable earnings to 66 and two-thirds. In 1977, they increased the number of weeks needed to qualify for UI from eight weeks to between 10 and 14 weeks. In 1979, they further reduced the benefit rate to 60 per cent.
The Liberals also began to require that some people pay back UI benefits and made a further increase to entrance requirements for new workers and people who had been laid off in the previous year. Finally, in 1980, the Liberals began to withdraw funding from UI and to shift more and more of the costs onto workers and employers.
Everything contained in this government legislation before us was ushered in by our Liberal colleagues in this House and by their colleagues in the Senate. There is no real friend of the unemployed there.
The Dalton gang, Barbara, Michael and Brian, have not spent much time riding the range since the bill was introduced. Perhaps the sun got into their eyes and has clouded their vision as to the desperate situation workers face in all parts of the country due to their free trade giveaway, tax grabs and cut-backs. Let us clear away the mist.
Since this bill was introduced, we have seen a crisis in the Atlantic fishery. Here the government proposes to get out of funding benefits for people engaged in fishing. The government proposes to use part of the premiums it collects in the Atlantic to pay for the Community Futures Program, a program the minister's own advisory committee says does not work very well. The minister, in defending her bill before the Senate, tells us that, according to her own experience, people in Newfoundland could find jobs if they had to. Maybe the minister has spent time looking for a job in Newfoundland and maybe she could share her experience with the Newfoundland Deputy Minister of Labour and tell him
March 12, 1990

where the jobs are, because he has said categorically that his studies show they do not exist.
In Ontario, with free trade sucking jobs south of the border, this government will put people off the UI rolls and onto the welfare rolls. That is not much of an improvement. It is not an improvement at all, because this government has just decided to cut payments for welfare because these people live in a rich province. I suspect that the people living in the rich province who will not be receiving unemployment insurance and who will be on welfare are really not aware how well off they are.
In Quebec, we have seen a significant rise in unemployment, but if this bill were in place today, thousands of workers there would have less time to find a job before their benefits ran out. In the west, in my own province of Saskatchewan, Premier Grant Devine has felt it necessary to put forward his own aid package as it is clear that the federal government has nothing to offer farmers in distress.
As I see it, this government has only one option. It is time to stop playing cowboys with the Senate and start taking responsibility for the mess they have made in this country. They should stop trying to blame unemployed workers for the crisis the government has created. This government never had a mandate to change UI legislation in the first place. It should introduce variable entrance requirement legislation to give relief to workers in areas of high unemployment. The government should accept the federal court ruling on parental benefits and introduce extended maternity benefits as well.
If it truly wants to support basic literacy training while people are on UI and support special benefits for people who fish, we will support it, providing that these initiatives are tied to variable entrance requirement legislation and not this harmful, poisonous bill.
Finally, the government and the Liberals should pack up their toys and call it a day. The Canadian people are tired of their games and, frankly, so are we. Someone has to tell this government enough is enough. Someone has to say no to a bill that cuts benefits to people who need them most, and no in response to the Senate, no to the
Government Orders
Liberals who have not listened and are no real friends of the unemployed, and a final no, because it is the fourth time closure has been introduced on this bill, an unprecedented disregard for democracy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I would like to rule on the admissibility of this motion, just in case the hon. member may have a subamendment. If he would please take his seat for a minute.
I believe the motion is in order. I will rule it admissible.

An hon. member from across the way stated: "the safety net of unemployment insurance and welfare programs is there just for the times we are now experiencing. Let us leave that safety net in place and recognize that there will be an increase in cost there". That is the quote from the hon. member across the way.
Will Michael remember his words, sit down with his colleagues, Barbara and Brian and stop trying to turn the social safety net into a tightrope?
In conclusion, I would reiterate that this bill must be withdrawn.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member who just spoke for some clarification. I am having a little difficulty understanding the position of the New Democratic Party on this. The member on the one hand disagrees with the Liberal Senate and on the other hand disagrees with the government and says the bill has to be withdrawn. That is very nice and we agree with him that the bill has to be withdrawn but the fact is the government is not withdrawing it.
We are dealing with a motion now to go back to the Senate. If the member had listened to the motion that was read he would realize that we are dealing with a government motion that purports to approve one of the Senate amendments but disapproves of the others. While we are reluctant to say that the Senate amendments are all that are needed to this dreadful bill, and we agree that it should be withdrawn, we have to deal with the motion now on the floor.

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
I am wondering if the member of the New Democratic Party by his participation in the debate today is urging the Senate of Canada to reject this bill and if he feels that that is an appropriate course.

I thank the member for the question, Mr. Speaker. What I am urging is that the government listen to what the Canadian public has said. I know the minister went through a long litany: "No, no, no." Repeating words three times can become a habit I guess. It is contagious.
The Canadian public told the government over and over again that these changes to unemployment insurance were absolutely unacceptable. The Canadian public told the government that to reduce the benefits which people would receive under unemployment insurance and to increase the amount of time a claimant had to work in order to qualify for them was unacceptable.
These changes, together with a smoke and mirrors explanation that education was going to be increased, left the implication that anyone who was unemployed, even anyone who never had a job, would be able to seek training now that the government was making these changes. Of course, that is patently untrue.
Although there may be a slight increase in the number of people who will be able to receive training as a result of the changes to the unemployment insurance, there was no assurance that anywhere near a significant number of people would receive any amount of significant training at all. As a matter of fact, if anything, it came to a point where they were dividing those who had never been employed and were hoping to find employment through training, and those who were insurably unemployed. The government is actually I think seeking to divide and conquer that way.
Certainly, for those who had never been employed the money that the government is now purporting to have available for them is money that it had previously put into unemployment insurance. It is now going to be giving to these people with no assurance that any significant number of people would be trained as a result of that, and no assurance that they would be able to find jobs as a result of that training. It is just the old game of smoke and mirrors.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Government House Leader):

As I understood the question,
the hon. member was asked whether or not he thought the Senate should reject this bill. I am really curious to hear the NDP position. It is a simple, straight question and I am wondering if the hon. member would answer it for us.
