March 12, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I have notice of closure to deliver:
I give notice that at the next sitting of the House, immediately before the Order of the Day is called for resuming debate on the motion of the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons in relation to amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, and on any amendments proposed thereto, I will move that the debate shall not be further adjourned.

Mr. Speaker, in recent months you have been exposed to impassioned rtheoric on Bill C-21. You have heard all kinds of comments, ranging from very objective on one side of the House to more subjective on the other. You have heard the worst epithets one can address to a piece of legislation. And a special committee of the other place was appointed to study our bill.
As was to be expected, a majority of the members of this committee condemned the intent of the changes we want to make in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Some of the proposals from the other place, Mr. Speaker, may be very worthwhile. In fact, this government has once again shown its flexibility by offering to accept certain amendments, including those on fishermen and literacy, areas we consider to be among our top priorities.
Unfortunately, a number of other recommendations were made without any thought for Canada's financial resources. It is easy to make commitments, especially when one is not elected and when managing Canada's economy is the least of one's concerns. This reminds me of the 1984 election campaign. In fact, Mr. Speaker, some of the senators who are opposed to Bill C-21 were part of the same government that left us with government finances in a very precarious state. Fortunately, since 1984, Canadians have opted for responsible government.
As I was saying, I remember the 1984 election campaign, when a party leader who has since left the House resorted to similar arguments during a televised debate: No, he said, not $30 million to improve the status of
Government Orders
women, but $300 million. Of course the Prime Minister's answer was: My friend, where is your magic wand?
You will recall that our ex-party leader quickly changed the subject.

Whoever said that history repeats itself was perhaps capable of time travel, because that is exactly what is happening in this House. Once again, our hon. colleagues in the other Chamber are suggesting a solution that would contribute to increasing the national debt: spending public funds wastefully. They have a regrettable tendency to assign a monetary value to a problem rather than seeking the problem's true cause and applying sound and lasting remedies.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit I have trouble understanding the logic of the liberal majority in the other place. On February 14, Senator Jacques Hebert told La Presse that the Liberal senators had no intention of having a long, drawn-out debate on Bill C-21.
In the same breath, Mr. Hebert said that personally, whatever his colleagues would do, he was ready for a long, hard fight. I simply don't understand.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that the House of Commons has a duty to consider a matter that concerns the majority of the citizens of this country. It is not a place for flaunting one's moods in front of the whole country.
Mr. Speaker, instead of designing strategies to break down the democratic process, the senators would have been well advised to really scrutinize the Bill before them. All of us on this side of the House know that political and economic observers in this country, while reasserting the need for training our manpower, recognize that the proposed changes will make unemployment insurance into the scheme it was intented to be in the first place. These observers recommend that we go ahead with Bill C-21. Opinion polls show the majority of Canadians are also in favour of this bill.
Unfortunately, we are back to where we started four months ago. In the meantime, our government had to abandon the idea of approving throughout the country variable entrance requirements for unemployment in-

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
surance benefits to claimants, wherever they live in Canada. Consequently, every worker must have worked 14 weeks before being eligible to benefits.
Mr. Speaker, every day, hundreds of people are denied their legitime right to UI benefits, because of little schemes like this, because of this obstruction which paralyzes the regular business of the House.
I simply cannot accept senator Hebert's comments about Bill C-21 not taking regional disparities into account.
The more the senators delay Bill C-21, the more harm they do to areas in Canada where unemployment is very high; the more they delay implementation of programs to reduce the gap denounced by Economic Council of Canada, the more the workers in these very regions will be penalized. Mr. Speaker, do we have to remind members that with Bill C-21 workers in regions with a high unemployment rate will be eligible to unemployment insurance benefits after only ten weeks of work?
If Bill C-21 had been enacted before January 1st, I know full well that the unemployed in areas with high unemployment would be treated more fairly.
Again, our reform is sensitive to fluctuations in the unemployment rate.

For example, in Comer Brook and Gander, Newfoundland, where the unemployment rate is in excess of 17 per cent, the variable entrance requirement prescribed by Bill C-21 would be reduced to 10 weeks instead of the 14 weeks currently in force. The same thing will apply in at least 14 other regions across the country.

Meanwhile, the democratically elected government has to wait for the other house, composed of non-elected senators, to let go of Bill C-21 and to let us take our responsabilities as members who have been elected to represent and manage this country.
By accusing the government of not taking regional disparities into account, the other house pleads ignorance and refuses to accept the democratic and economic changes that have occurred in our country over the past 12 years.
Again, the variable entrance requirement, which is one of the main amendments proposed in Bill C-21, takes regional disparities into account. One really has to wonder if senators have read the bill.
Mr. Speaker, when we announced our intention to end the tripartite funding of unemployment insurance, the Liberals in the other place once again tried to stir up the masses. Without going into the reasons why we were stopping our contributions to the UI Fund, they cried treason and claimed that the government was "abandoning ship".
I just heard an explanation that is totally false. Our decision to withdraw from UI funding has absolutely nothing to do with the free trade agreement that we signed. Once again, it is obvious that they have not done their homework. How can the government fund UI? Go on borrowing year after year, thereby increasing the deficit and the taxes to pay this growing debt? That is totally absurd and irresponsible. Another falsehood coming from my colleagues opposite and in the other place is that UI will be cut. That is really overstating and misrepresenting it. How many times do we have to repeat that Bill C-21 will not reduce the scope of the UI Plan at all? We are not cutting anything. Instead, we want to reallocate $800 million from the UI Fund to training programs and assistance for relocation, entrepreneurship and re-employment. This is no doubt the measure which best illustrates the distinction our government makes between funding active and passive measures. Providing funds to maintain the dependency of recipients on the state is a passive measure.

Upgrading advisory services, providing access to courses, and paying extended benefits to those who participate in training programs: such measures are what we mean when we talk about giving an active aspect to one of the most important programs in Canada. We believe that it is unacceptable for employers to be short of qualified labour at the same time so many people are looking for fulfilling jobs.
Even in my riding we are searching for these kinds of people. We are seeking to introduce strategies and mechanisms designed to encourage beneficiaries to get off the Catch-22 and achieve financial independence. As
March 12, 1990

many people have understood, we are stressing longterm lasting solutions.

The late Felix Leclerc appreciated the irony of a certain kind of government we will have no part of. "The best way to kill a man" he used to say, "is to pay him for not working". Our mandate is to find ways to help the unemployed find in themselves the resources that will change them into more dynamic individuals, because the challenges ahead require the involvement of this country's total human resources.
Mr. Speaker, if that political will of ours keeps on being labeled an abdication of our responsibilities, as the other place suggests, this is bad faith and bad partisanship.

I would like to mention another set of changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act which millions of Canadians are impatiently waiting to see adopted. I am talking about the in-depth changes to the current maternity, sickness, and parental benefits program. These matters are of special importance to me. Because of the important human dimension of the relevant measures in Bill C-21-

The bill provides for the maintenance of 15 weeks of maternity benefits during the period surrounding childbirth. Added to this are an extra 10 weeks of parental benefits to natural or adoptive parents. Under the flexible provisions of the new legislation in some cases the total period of combined maternity, parental and sickness benefits available to parents could be extended up to 30 weeks.
What did the special committee of the other place have to say on that? A lot of good, blended with the cynicism that permeates the whole report. The government should have done so much sooner, or so they said. My answer is that this government works seriously, using in depth analysis and, more importantly, consultations with all the parties involved. When the government decides to bring in amendments, it does not do so within the narrow context of a single aspect of the Act. This is
Government Orders
because, quite simply, all the provisions in the Act are interdependent.
Our concern as far as the unemployment insurance is concerned, goes back many years ago, following the tabling of the Forget Commission's report whose findings did not probably meet the expectations of the time. Then there were the Grandpre Commission's recommendations which greatly inspired the government's Labour Force Development Strategy. The very thorough consultations carried out by this Commission throughout Canada had emphasized the urgent need to intensify the training and retraining of our labour force, in order to fully benefit from all the opportunities created by the Europe 92 free trade accord, in short, the globalization of world markets.
Our Labour Force Development Strategy is made up of an admittedly rather complex package of measures the scope of which compels us to look beyond the beginning of the 21st Century. It would be asking too much than to expect the unconditional support of the other place whose members include many who have been influenced throughout their lives by governments whose views did not go beyond their constituents' immediate concerns. That was really the issue over these past few months, during the endless debates surrounding the proposed amendments to the unemployment insurance legislation.
As other government speakers, I have tried to convince the elected and non-elected oppositions that all our actions dealing with labour-related issues will now be interconnected. The amendements to Bill C-21, therefore, are no exception, because they are consistent with the main themes which presided over the establishment of our Labour Force Development Strategy.
Employers' and employees' organizations have all expressed almost the same concern. Morally, we do not have the right to let our labour force lag behind that of other industrialized nations. As competition intensifies, it would be a mistake to close our eyes to the reality of world markets.
Training, retraining, skill improvement, increased flexibility on the part of both employers and employees are all vital concerns shared by public and private sector major representatives. But how could we meet their demands if the other place puts us in a totally disabling legislative straitjacket?

March 12, 1990
Government Orders

The time for discussion is past. It is time to act. We are trying to implement the principle which we have stated but, yet again, the other place is blocking us at every turn.
I deplore that we are being prevented from taking our responsibilities as the lawfully elected government. Time is running out and we are still not doing enough to give Canadians the tools they need to handle the challenges of the 21st century. It is unacceptable that for months at a time we should be forced to discuss the spirit and the letter of any proposed amendment to an act. I feel that we are currently being forced to take part in a pointless masquerade. I am very much afraid that this endless argument is making a mockery of the democratic exercise of power.

Ultimately, the government alone must be held responsible for actions it takes with full knowledge of the facts.
If time proves us wrong, we will bear the consequences according to the rules of the game. But our policies will have to be judged by the people, not by an unelected partisan group who tarnishes the reputation of an institution.
Mr. Speaker, I ask my colleages to make every effort to bring this debate to an end as soon as possible.
Thousands of people, employers, unemployed, unemployment insurance claimants, workers over 65, workers who desperately need training, in short the whole working community, are watching the House of Commons.
I am confident that if we take the proper decisions, in the interest of the majority, we will make up for the time that has been lost and help give Canada back the dynamism that has so often and so eloquently marked its history.

Madam Minister, we have met this morning in caucus representatives from all Canadian labour unions from coast to coast. You mentioned earlier that workers seem to support the government regarding this Bill and asked us not to allow the Senate to block the passage of the Bill. This morning however, the unions and their representatives begged us to make sure to ask the Senate to kill that legislation which they consider as
somewhat prompted by the US because they see it as a subsidy. What do you think of all the unions in our country stating that you are yielding to US entreaties on account of the free trade deal? Does that not bother you that all the workers in this country have asked for the opposite of what you have asked this House?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
First I must say that we are not reacting to what the United States are asking us to do. When we began the unemployment insurance reform we knew full well that skilled workers are in very short supply and that the reform would enable us to improve the skills of workers while they seek employment. I have here an article from my riding where the unemployment rate is unfortunately too high, 15 to 20 per cent, and where people say it is not easy to find skilled labour. They are trying to get a paper mill going and looking hard for workers, carpenters, welders and plumbers. Everybody wants them, but there are not enough qualified men and women. We are talking about plumbers and welders, and these are trades for which workers could be retrained. The government is aware that we need direct training.
We know very well that our system is too passive, that we must make it more active. And we also know full well that we need this reform to create longer-lasting jobs for the future to be able to compete on tomorrow's market. The reform has to be a concerted effort on the part of employers, employees and the private sector, and that is what we are working on. It is a reform, and in its latest report the Economic Council of Canada again stressed the need for more training, and they even suggetsed that our active unemployment insurance scheme be turned into a work insurance system. As a responsible government that is what we have been working on since 1984. At long last this reform will enhance the skills and abilities of Canadian workers. Wherever the unemployment rate is high our reform takes into account the particularities of each region. There is no reason why we should apologize for a bill which comes to grips with the reality and which was drafted after consultation with the various interests of the private sector, the employers and the employees.

Mr. Speaker, the minister referred to helping workers in her last response. I would like to ask the minister a couple of questions. One, how will the forcing of workers to pay for training benefits help those workers in the future?
March 12, 1990

The government pays a share of that training cost and it is now talking about privatizing. In fact, Bill C-21 does privatize training and puts the burden of training on the backs of the workers and their employers. That may be the kind of active, as opposed to passive, effort the minister is talking about, the workers cariying that burden on their shoulders as opposed to the government sharing that burden.
The minister referred to the Economic Council of Canada asking for these changes. I have heard suggested today that the Canadian Labour Congress and the labour coalition are interest groups that do not represent what the government wants represented. Second, I would like to ask whose interests the Economic Council of Canada represents and why the government is listening to them instead of the four million workers the coalition of unions represents who presented their views today and the government would not hear?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are listening to the workers. Before going into politics in 1984,1 worked with employees in the professional sector. There is a growing need for training across Canada. With unemployment insurance reform, we are trying to put in place a labour force development strategy.
Unemployed workers do not pay for their own training. On the contrary, it is employers and workers who are paying for an insurance against future hardships.
As we know full well-and I'm sure you will agree with me-, all social workers admit that training must be provided and that co-operation is essential. That is what we are trying to do. We must ensure that the government has a role to play but that the strategy is defined by the private sector. That is why we have set up advisory committees to give us a training strategy. We are trying to meet current needs while preparing for the year 2000. We, Canadian men and women, must be competitive in the new markets and be ready to face these new challenges.

Mr. Speaker, I am really at a loss for words when I listen to the minister give an explanation of what should be taking place in the employment sector. She has been represent-
Govemment Orders
ing the government sector for five years and recognizes the problems of underemployment, lack of skills training, and lack of skilled workers. She can stand there for five minutes explaining that now, after the government has cut out $770 million over the last five years in training programs, it has seen the light and is going to talk about what it is going to do with our labour market.
I cannot believe that the minister actually has an ounce of sincerity when talking about what we have to do in the country with our labour pool. She admits that in her own riding she has an unemployment rate of approximately 15 per cent. The only thing I can say is shame on her and shame on the government for the kinds of conditions that she is decrying. She has been in a position to do something about them over the last five years. It is a lot of poppycock and claptrap that we are hearing from this government.
One thing that should be made very clear, and there is no one in the House who does not believe it, is that we have to become more competitive by having a better trained labour market and that the government has to be proactive. It does not become proactive by turning around, cutting training programs, getting out of the labour market, getting out of its contribution and commitment, its fiduciary trust that it has in this particular program, and then stand up before this House, saying say that it represents all kinds of Canadians. A coalition that represents 4 million labourers in the country asked us to do something to get the government to pay attention.
Members of the government stand up and read the same speeches we heard at second reading, report stage, and third reading. I can see the parliamentary secretary to the minister here doing the same thing. He listens to the same stuff that we have been listening to over the course of the very little bit of debate that we were allowed.
I cannot believe that a government which asks for support at the same time turns around and, at the very first instance that we can have an opportunity to discuss this on substance, says: "We are going to impose closure once again". Let's stop this nonsense. If we are going to have a debate on substance let us get onto it. Let us get busy and talk about what we have to do with the unemployed.

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
Maybe, just maybe, it would be instructive for members on the government side to understand who the unemployed are in this country. If we are going to be talking about doing something with our labour market, then let us see what we have to do. Let us take a look at the figures that it has to address if, in fact, it is going to have any basis for making some of the assumptions that it is going to make.
Quite frankly, over the course of the last five years we have seen an enormous decline in the creation of good jobs. I pointed this out earlier this morning in a statement in the House. The government refuses to recognize that the free trade agreement has anything to do with the realities of the moment but we have lost 9,700 full time, good, solid jobs. These are the kinds of jobs that the minister says are lacking in her own riding. She cannot get plumbers, she cannot get welders. Where in the heck has she been for the last five years as a representative of the government? If the government is going to do something, do something worth while. Do not give us this garbage saying: "We are going to put $800 million into training".
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what that $800 million represents? It is coming out of premiums that are paid by both employees and employers. The government is washing its hands of the whole affair. What it is doing is increasing the proportion of moneys that it is going to take out of those premium payments in order to finance the obligations that it should have been meeting under Canadian Jobs Strategy programs.
For the edification of the members opposite, I add that the Estimates indicate that funding under CJS is approximately $1.5 billion. If the government goes through with Bill C-21, it will make itself a predator of up to an additional 15 per cent of funds from those premiums, funds that will equal $1.8 billion.
I dare say that if we are going to be talking about confidences and trust, then the parliamentary secretary opposite will attest to the veracity of what has been going on. Moneys have been removed from government contributions and taken from premiums to be allocated where? To those same programs that are still being cut. The government looked at a surplus in the unemployment
insurance scheme last year, ruled that is was surplus and said: "We are going to remove our contribution".
The parliamentary secretary knows that quite well. His minister stood up before the House and said: "You know what? We have to reform the unemployment insurance system". Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? Because we are in a deficit situation, not because we need to develop our labour market nor because we are getting together with private enterprise and labour.
Madam Minister might pay careful attention that those groups who called for complete withdrawal of Bill C-21 this morning represent 4 million Canadians. She does not need them. Her party does not need them. Her government does not need them. It does not need anybody. It is standing at 19 per cent in the polls, but that is okay. They are non-believers anyway. Maybe, in the next election, many of those people of the 4 million and up will take a look at what is going on with this particular bill, and the debate on this bill, and will decide to teach the government a lesson in numbers.
Certainly the government has indicated that it cares not a whit about literacy programs. It cares not a whit about preparing those workers who are in a disadvantaged position throughout the entire country. I do not know how many times we have stood before the House and pointed out to the Minister of Employment and the Minister of State that the illiteracy rate in this country among adults is one of the highest in the western world. We cannot possibly be competitive unless we address it.
What does the minister do? What does the Minister of Finance do in his latest budget? Cut programs. Where? Where they hurt most and where they do the greatest damage. We had an opportunity to do something for native Canadians, for Canadians of all origins and for Canadians who are crying for some kind of government program, direction and vision that says: "Look, we are going to provide a job". What kind of job? This is the government that five years ago said: "We are going to create jobs, jobs, jobs". What kind of jobs have we got? We have a 45 per cent increase in the kinds of jobs that are part-time, dead-end, marginal, seasonal and rely on help agencies.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism ought to be interested in this. He is one of the guys who is defending a 7 per cent increase in the goods and services tax that is going to do a heck of a lot to destroy
March 12, 1990

even those types of jobs that are maintained by an unemployment insurance system. They give an opportunity to provide people with the occasion to live in their area of origin and preference in this country, and maintain the population in the regions of Canada not close to Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and some of the other major centres.
We have to do something reasonable and worth while to maintain the opportunity of Canadians to move around the country, Canadians with full rights, full opportunities and full access to the equalities of the occasions and opportunities provided by our government. If our government is to make a sincere effort to ensure that all Canadians have equality of access then it has to be serious about an educational training program that takes into consideration the obligation to do what is right, to do what it must do in order to develop an industrial labour policy for all Canadians. My colleague from Saskatoon-Dundurn, who served on the legislative committee with me, knows very well that even those skilled labourers in Saskatchewan have very little opportunity in terms of finding a job in their own areas, even if they are skilled.
In times of recession such as this, there are, on average, 2,000 labourers per month leaving that province looking for greener pastures elsewhere. They will not find those greener pastures in Toronto where the average house costs $272,000 and where one needs a $70,000 down payment to qualify for a mortgage.
I do not know if we can take seriously some of the arguments we have heard from the other side of the House. The House leader talks about the illegitimate nature of the resolution of the Senate which states that the bill is fraught with problems and it is going to make the bill a little more palatable.
The minister says that the Senate has the legal and constitutional right but should not exercise it. I have never heard such garbage in my life. This government must think that everybody is stupid. It is certainly operating as if Canadians do not care. Canadians have a stake in this country and they want to see the government take action to ensure that their future is secure, that their future looks auspicious down the road and provides an opportunity for their kids as well as for every other person's kids.
Government Orders
There is a lack of concern and arrogant disdain with which the government treats all arguments regarding the variable entrance requirements, absolute scorn which it heaps on members on this side of the House, and I dare say from the NDP as well, who indicate there are some positive ways in which this government can give some kind of direction and purpose. That kind of scorn cannot be allowed to continue, especially under the guise of fighting members of the other place who have a duty, an obligation and a constitutional right to throw this bill back into the lap where it belongs. The Senate says: "Look, get it done and get it done right".
The government refuses to acknowledge a constitutional obligation in law, as well as in practice. Since 1941, the Unemployment Insurance Commission, our whole social security system, that income maintenance system that is the unemployment insurance, requires three parties: labour, industry and the government. But our government cavalierly opts out of its obligation. I do not know of a Canadian who would turn around and say "Yes, I applaud that because it allows you to pilfer some money out of the fund and to reduce a deficit which you have been so lax and incompetent in handling over the last five years".
I cannot believe that there would be one Canadian who would say that this government recognizes constitutionality. It pompously indicates through the House leader that it is the oracle of truth and that it understands constitutionality.
I cannot believe that there would be one Canadian who would for one moment accept a government that takes more than 3 per cent from the contributions to the fund and raises that to 15 per cent and accepts that that would be a constitutional, legal or moral thing to do. I am sorry if I mention morality. It is something that obviously is not in the vocabulary of members on the government side. Members opposite are probably ignorant when it comes to looking up that definition in the dictionary. Lest I become too sarcastic and I do not want to stray from the item at hand, the purpose of this particular debate is to point out that the other House has done the House of Commons and the people of Canada an enormous favour by suggesting that this bill be reviewed in its entirety. We should not be concentrating merely on the variable entrance requirement. This thing is flawed in principle because it does away with the whole

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
concept of government responsibility in the area of income maintenance and social security.
Government members opposite have laughed and they have scorned. They have put down any interventions by members on this side of the House who have suggested that perhaps there has to be a reason, a rationale, some sort of philosophy behind the government's desire to kill a system that has been an integral part of the Canadian character.
What is that objective? What is that philosophy? My friends on this side of the House, I think know only too well. They read the papers, but we are not allowed to accept them as any source of veracity. They read all the documentation that comes forward from the government researchers, from government institutions, from government departments, but we are not allowed to accept those as any sources of truth. The Minister of State for Employment and Immigration just told us: "Well, listen, none of that stuff matters". We cannot go to those areas. We cannot talk to our own researchers who tell us what Americans tell us, that is, with this bill the government is intending to ensure that our social security system falls in line with the American system.
What is it designed to do? It is designed to take into consideration all the negotiations regarding subsidies and to pre-empt any discussions on subsidies that we should be conducting sincerely and properly for the interest of all Canadians.
If there is any other reason, then all we have to do is listen to the minister's own words when she said: "We are only doing this because we have to cut the deficit". It is either one or the other. They are going to cut the deficit on the backs of all those Canadians who have relied on this because they have contributed to it. They have paid taxes to maintain a system of social security because they felt that was an obligation on their part as taxpayers and Canadians. They have done that as employers and as employees because they felt that was their obligation under this tripartite agreement.
We have a government with such arrogance that it turns around and not only walks away from the deal but then spits in the plate from which it has eaten and says: "We are doing this for your own good". If it is doing this for our own good, the best thing that it could possibly do
is to pack up and resign. Passing bills such as this in jack-boot fashion, closure after closure after closure, and then coming in here and giving us this poppycock about a hundred hours of debate across country is just absolutely mind boggling. There is not a Canadian out there who actually believes for a moment that these people are capable of telling the truth. There is not a one.
At no time like the present do we need pro-active legislation by a Government of Canada. I see none in this bill from this Government of Canada. I see none coming out of that ministry, that department which says that it shall create conditions, not only that will decrease unemployment but improve the level and quality of employment.
The minister sits here and tells this House that because there is 15 per cent unemployment in her riding and because there are one or two positions available for plumbers and welders that this is absolutely shameful. She says that we are going to make sure that over one million Canadians who find themselves in the unfortunate position of being either underemployed or unemployed bear the brunt of the government's desire to cut the deficit at the expense of all those who rely on a system in order to maintain whatever lifestyle that they have in whatever part of Canada.
I am not talking about people who live in St. Paul's or Forest Hill or Rosedale. I am talking about average Canadians, average Canadians who are quite happy to work daily, to take on part-time jobs. I pointed out that there has been a 45 per cent increase in the types of jobs being taken by people who feel a need to take on a second job to maintain their lifestyle.
Those people are crying for an industrial and economic strategy that is sorely and evidently lacking in this legislation. Yet the department, the government, the Prime Minister and his cabinet have decided they are going to take this club called Bill C-21 and with that club they are going to beat into submission all of us who are so unfortunate as to find ourselves at the mercy of those who would give us, at their whim and their will, the kind of jobs that are going to decrease in number progressively, as we have seen with the increase in the unemployment rate steadily over the course of this year, and in quality.
March 12, 1990

I thank you for your patience, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry that my time is running out. I would have loved to have given more to the parliamentary secretary.

What the government has to decide, and I can tell my hon. friend through you, Mr. Speaker, that it is no longer a question of simply saying, as my esteemed colleague opposite says: "This is a provincial matter. speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that it is nice to speak in the House where there is a little chat-back and a little bit of action.
I rise in support of the motion put forward by the government House leader. While there are some ideas which we can agree with in the message from the other place, there is a basic conflict between most of these amendments and the intent of Bill C-21.
Bill C-21 has been held up long enough. The needs it addresses are too important to justify prolonged argument over detail. For this reason we believe that the responsible course is to recognize valid concerns of the Senate. However there are recommendations proposed by the Senate which we cannot accommodate. I want to discuss these briefly now, starting with amendment 2(a) (b) and (c).
The government is determined to do more than passively accept unemployment. We must help unemployed people get back to work and make it possible for them to contribute to the growth of this country. For this reason we have proposed to expand the present uses of unemployment insurance to provide training for more people, to allow for more people to retrain their skills
March 12, 1990

while unemployed and to help people get back to work faster.
Basically the Senate amendment says that it is okay for the government to use unemployment insurance funds to write income support cheques but not for anything else. In other words, they close the door on the so-called developmental uses. To put it less bureaucratically, they close the door on helping people to do more than just survive on unemployment.
A main goal of Bill C-21 is to assist the return to the workforce of people for whom unemployment is not an unchangeable fact of life but a condition which could be changed if certain obstacles were removed.
For instance, people who live in depressed areas where there are no jobs could move to areas where there are jobs, if they could only come up with the money to do so.
For instance, there are people who could find work in their own communities, if only they had the necessary skills.
For instance, unemployed experienced, energetic UI eligible people could realistically be self-employed if they could only get the helping hand to get started, people who in the long run might create more jobs for others.
Under Bill C-21 the government should have the option of using money from the UI funds to help people over these hurdles-to pay for training, to help with moving expenses, and to help launch small businesses.
Let us all be clear on two points. First, the funds spent this way would be well invested. A few thousand dollars spent in one year conceivably could save tens of thousands of dollars in future claims over the years. Second, given the deficit, this funding cannot be financed out of general revenues. The Liberal Senate amendments before this House obstruct these-
And you are putting them out of work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Do you want to rise and speak? Why don't you not get up on your feet and speak?
Government Orders
The Liberal Senate amendments before this House obstruct these principles in general and in detail by insisting that we fund them from the central revenues where no money is available, and they would kill them at birth. In the case of relocation assistance, they require that no one be helped to move to an area with better opportunities until there is a firm job offer on the table, but this creates a catch-22 situation. How likely is it that an unemployed worker at one end of the country will be able to line up a definite job at the other end of the country? We would like to be more flexible and more realistic in this regard.
Amendment 3 from the other place deals with the right of appeal. We have such a right at the present time. If you believe you are a victim of an unsound decision about UI benefits you can appeal to the board of referees. This amendment goes further. It would extend the right of appeal beyond the benefits to the new developmental uses.
This is mixing apples and oranges. The question as to whether I entitled tox number of dollars for* number of weeks under the act when it arises lends itself to a judicial resolution.
Questions about whether a move to a given area at a given time will improve job prospects or whether training will be productive involve the informed judgment of counsellors in consultation with applicants. They must relate to the circumstances which vary. This amendment would complicate decision making. It would obstruct counselling. It would slow down the process to no useful end. The people who would be hurt the most would be unemployed Canadians trying to get back to work.
Amendments 4(B), (C) and (D) from the other place are also for the most part unhelpful but with modification provide basis for agreement. The Senate wants us to specify year by year, province by province, economic region by economic region, what we will spend on developmental use, and where we will spend it. They want an accounting after the fact that we can provide. They want a detailed account before the fact not only for each of the 10 provinces but for each economic region. We believe in planning too, and Bill C-21 allows for it within the limits of practicality and reality. It is pretty difficult to look into an area before the fact and in some of the remote areas in particular to try to estimate what is going to happen there.

March 12, 1990
Government Orders
The reality is that between the time you make your plan and the time the new fiscal year comes around situations can change, and they can change quite dramatically. Markets can change. Product lines and skill requirements can change. Superimpose that on the fact that for UI planning purposes there are no less than 62 economic regions in Canada, each with different needs and situations. Locking yourself into too detailed a blueprint, one drawn up a year in advance, is not the way to meet those needs effectively. To be truly and effectively responsible we need the flexibility that Bill C-21 provides.
It comes to this: we cannot agree to a proposal that would set plans in stone a year ahead and which in any case would be speculative. We are prepared to meet the concerns expressed in the Senate amendment by elaborating the yearly plan to incorporate more detail but not beyond the limits of what is practical. That means an estimate, not a plan covering the 10 provinces and the 2 territories.
Amendment 4 (D) would make the planning process a political football. Each plan each year would be the subject of a debate in both Houses subject to rejection by either or both.
Furthermore, we note that if either House does not act within 10 sitting days the regulations would expire. In short, we are asked to approve not only the hobbling of the planning machinery, but to sanction a veto by the other place on regulations that can affect the livelihood of thousands of Canadians who need our help.
Amendment 5(A) from the other place concerns the qualification period for people who, without just cause, leave one job to go to another.
Here again distinctions are essential. Many people who quit their jobs in this way do so because of intolerable conditions or other compelling circumstances. There are many reasons a person should be allowed to leave a job without a penalty. That is not the issue. The issue is not even the right of anyone at any time to quit a job without just cause. The issue is whether the people who do so should be supported by all the people who pay unemployment insurance premiums, whether these people should pay a bill which has been running at more than $1 billion a year.
The related issue is whether the deterrents now in place to discourage this practice are effective. Bill C-21 will increase the deterrents. One way it will do it is by setting the disqualification period at seven to twelve weeks. The amendments proposed by the Liberal senators on the other hand favour the status quo. They would keep the deterrents at their present inadequate level. In effect they support those who want to use UI as a free ride at everyone else's expense.
Amendment 6 from the other place is about third party contracting. Bill C-21 envisages the use of third party contractors to services such as training administration. Logically, we say, their operations should be funded from the same source as Canada Employment centre administration, from the general UI fund. The Senate amendment would require these administrative expenses to be paid out of the 15 per cent portion of the UI fund earmarked for training relocation and other development uses. Obviously every dollar spent on administration would be $1 less for developmental measures. We do not think that is a good amendment.
Amendment 7 from the other place runs counter to one of the main goals of Bill C-21, namely, to train more workers and counter the wider consideration of reducing the federal deficit. In the April 1989 budget the government announced its decision to put UI on a self-supporting basis. Continuing to support it from general revenues is not an option that is consistent with cutting the deficit. The money just is not there.
In effect Bill C-21 says that those who benefit from the UI program should pay for it. That means not just Canadian workers but Canadian employers. The Senate amendments reject that approach. It says that drafters are "mindful of the government's stated goal of deficit control". Mindful or not, it requires that the government, a convenient euphemism for the Canadian taxpayer, should shoulder 50 per cent of the cost of what are commonly referred to as regional benefits.
This amendment is inconsistent with deficit reduction. It contradicts the principle that programs should be paid for by those who benefit from them; in this case employers and employees. We have an even more basic problem with this proposal. The House of Commons cannot accept an argument which essentially says that although the government has the constitutional right to reduce the deficit in abstract terms, the right evaporates
March 12, 1990

when we get to specifics, that the Senate can stop the government from cutting the deficit by reducing spending on any given program. We cannot tolerate that.
I pass now to Amendment 9 from the other place. The situation of commercial fishermen in Atlantic Canada particularly is virtually unique. Their work is seasonal. Their resource base and their markets are fickle. The industry is plagued with overcapacity. The uniqueness of the fishing industry is recognized in the unemployment insurance system. Special regulations cover the people who work in it. The continued existence of these regulations is not in question. The issue is whether we should accept the proposition that these regulations be subject to review, debate and approval or rejection in the House of Commons and the Senate. The issue is whether we give the Senate a new power under the Unemployment Insurance Act, the power to veto these regulations. That change is neither necessary nor desirable.
Senate amendment No. 9 concerns the funding of fishermen's UI programs. At present, fishermen put in $1 of UI premiums for every $20 they draw out in benefits. That is a function of instability, which it goes with the territory. The issue is which particular funding source the money should come from.
To sum up, some of the ideas coming to us from the other place merit consideration. We can accept them without difficulty. Others run 180 degrees counter to the intent of this government and, more important, to the will of this elected House. We want to move to a solvent soundly-based system and do so in ways consistent with reducing the deficit. These amendments obstruct that effort.
We want to modernize the system to meet current needs. These amendments cling to the status quo. We want a more flexible system and these amendments would entrench rigidity. We want to remove disincentives from the system and these amendments would perpetuate them. We want the UI to function both as a bridge back to employment, and as an important income support. These amendments run counter to that goal. We want to address the urgent national need to develop our human resources to meet the needs and the challenges of the decade ahead. These amendments ignore that issue.

Finally, we want the will of the elected members of this House to prevail. These amendments would frustrate that will. For all these reasons, I support this motion by the government House leader and I urge my fellow members to do the same thing.

Mr. Speaker, just a few words concerning the resolution before the House today. I must say the reaction of the Government of Canada to the Senate proposals is really one that says it does not care about the unemployed in Canada. The Government of Canada, by reacting the way it has to the Senate proposal, is saying that it wants to cut people out of the unemployment insurance system.
March 12, 1990

The Government of Canada wants to discriminate against people from one part of this country. It does not care about the high unemployment areas of Canada. Bill C-21, should really be entitled "What side of the line do you live on"?
The government has refused to address the issue in its response to the Senate. Under the previous legislation, a repeater, which is what the majority of people are, and if they lived in an area where the unemployment rate was higher than 11.5 per cent, in order to qualify for unemployment insurance they needed only 2.5 months in a qualifying period.
Under this bill, if you live in a region of Canada in which the unemployment rate is below 15 per cent, you need more than 10 weeks to qualify. That is quite a basic change, is it not? That is quite a saving of money by the Government of Canada.
Under the existing law, if you live in an area in which the unemployment rate was below 11.5 per cent, you need more than 10 weeks to qualify. Under this bill, if you live in a region in which the unemployment rate is less than 15 per cent, you need more than 10 weeks to qualify.
The Senate objected to the fact that the government has rewritten the unemployment insurance boundary lines in Canada. In other words, when a person now walks into the unemployment insurance office, under this legislation the unemployment insurance officer will ask where that person lives. Never before was that question asked in a high unemployment area. The unemployment rate in high unemployment areas undoubtedly was always over 11.5 per cent. But now, with this change, in an area that has less than 15 per cent unemployment you need more than 10 weeks; over 15 per cent, you need 10 weeks.
The government decided to rearrange the lines. It put a metropolitan area in the middle of a zone so that if you live two miles away from a city, then you are going to need what they need in the city to qualify. Then it drew other lines in each province in such a way that it separated economic zones.
Let us look at high unemployment areas, for example. People there work on a boat on the high seas; a lake boat in central Canada; an airplane that flies over the ocean.
Government Orders
They work in the woods in the middle of nowhere; or in a mine somewhere. That is regional employment. Mr. Speaker, I have just told you what the vast majority of people do in the high unemployment areas. They do not work in their community. They work in areas away from their community. Invariably that is the case.
Now, under this new legislation, you qualify depending on where you live. Let us take, for example, a group of people who are working in the forests and have to apply for UI under this new legislation. If they live along a short stretch of road at Northern Arm, one small community and Phillips Head, another community a mile away, the qualifying UI rate varies. You qualify in one community but you do not qualify in the next community.
It is discrimination based upon where you live. It neglects the fact that the majority of people in rural areas of high unemployment do not work where they live. That, Mr. Speaker, is what the Government of Canada failed to address in the proposal from the Senate.
The Senate, in its response, went half way and said there is too much of a problem in making qualifications depend on each province and on which side of the line one lives on.
The Government of Canada drew the lines in a very unusual fashion. In Newfoundland it drew it along the old roadbed of the railway. We have heard the expression, "Which side of the tracks do you live on?". That expression, under this new legislation, really hits home because now it is "which side of the roadbed do you live on?"
Depending on what side of the line one lives, if you do not have enough weeks to qualify, the government has a training program in which you can qualify. That is, if you have not worked for the previous 30 weeks you can qualify to be trained for something. Someone who works in the woods cannot go into the training program to learn anything about the woods. That person has to learn about something else like carpentry, or electricity for the next 16 weeks, at a low wage.
For those who do qualify under this legislation, the government will apply clause 21 of this legislation, which is not insurable employment at all. You end up at the end of the system, on welfare.
