Mr. Speaker, I would like to pursue a question I raised in this House concerning criminal organizations that use modem financial services to hide the illegal source of their funds, and the means at the disposal of governments and financial institutions to control to some extent those transactions by making money laundering activities more difficult for criminals and to help enforcement bodies.
Mr. Speaker, billions of dollars of drugs profits cross the Canada-US border each year in order to be laundered in this country's financial institutions.
The process will accelerate as the United States strengthen their money-laundering control legislation in their jurisdiction.
As you know, the existing legislation in Cqpgda does not address that problem. The Banks Act includes some provisions on setting up and maintaining information files, as do the acts regulating other financial institutions.
However, the kinds of information kept in those files are those required by banking practices, rather than those that would indeed point to typical money-laundering transactions.
The Act includes no disclosure provisions, and under the current legislation, financial institutions that would disclose information would be in violation of banking confidentiality or other such rules concerning the disclosure of personal financial information.
This means that existing provisions serve to protect the banks rather than help law enforcement.
Mr. Speaker, over these last 15 years, studies on organized crime done mainly in United States but also in Canada, the United Kingdom and the Australia by those
who are seeking ways to control the power and wealth of criminal organizations have emphasized the important role of financial institutions in this regard.
In order to make use of the enormous sums of money they earn illegally, criminals must go through financial services, and in fact they have turned to financial institutions that also serve legitimate businesses.
It is extremely difficult to differentiate legal funds from illegal funds when a series of financial transactions are quickly processed through international financial networks.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the tradition of bank secrecy which surrounds financial transactions contributes to the problem, especially when funds arrive in countries where their identity is protected by strict laws on bank secrecy.
In 1970, the U.S. Congress passed a law obliging financial institutions to keep certain files and to declare certain financial transactions, namely monetary transactions of over $10,000 and the entry into or exit from the United States of amounts of $5,000 or more.
As you know, there are civil and criminal penalties for violations.
Bill C-61 contains measures to fight the laundering of the proceeds of organized crime as well as serious drug offences and the possession of goods obtained as a result of such offences.
The decision to criminalize the laundering of drug money and seize the bank assets of persons suspected of drug trafficking has made it possible to reduce the flood of hundreds of millions of dollars that were going through banks in Toronto and Montreal but, as you know, implementation of these control measures remains inadequate.
According to a recent report tabled in the U.S. Senate, last October American banks pointed to a surprising difference between the outflow of funds to Canada, estimated at $1.5 billion and the inflow of Canadian funds into the United States, which totalled over $4.5 billion.
This Bill does not oblige banks or other financial institutions to register and report to the authorities all major cash or foreign currency transactions.
March 12, 1990

Without ways to detect transactions involving major sums of illicit money, it is difficult to implement legislation against money laundering.
According to a report from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, corruption in the banking system is not unusual.
An unscrupulous bank manager even helped a major group of heroin traffickers buy bank drafts for a value exceeding $40 million. These drafts where then deposited in various financial institutions abroad.
In other cases, lower-ranked employees open and manage bank accounts at their place of work in order to launder drug money. The city of Drummondville even seconded a member of its police force to the RCMP to protect a mafia informant who testified on Canadian and Quebec television that it was very easy to transfer money between American and Canadian banks.
Consequently, whatever the means used, once drug money gets in the banking system, it can be tranferred almost immediately, anywhere in the world by the sophisticated electronic equipment used by financial institutions. The police is aware of such transactions, but has no power to act. As for the financial institutions, they prefer to turn a blind eye than to risk loosing a client to a competitor. So, the minister announced on January 18 the establishment of a joint government and private sector advisory committee on money laundering. Such initiative certainly is a step forward in the battle against traffickers. In Switzerland, as you know, they have what they call the "Convention de diligence", a kind of gentleman's agreement between bankers. By virtue of that agreement, they are required to ascertain that their client is truly the holder of his capital and to know its origin.
However, to work around the agreement it only takes a lawyer or a trust company to open an account on behalf of their client using the protection provided by professional secrecy.
So, flaws still exist in spite of measures put in place. Mr. Speaker, my question to the Hon. Minister of State for Finance is this: to engage a real fight against the power and the wealth of criminal organizations, what action will Canada consider with regards to regulated and non regulated financial institutions, the small cashing services and currency exchange facilities insceasingly
Adjournment Debate
used by those organizations, along with international electronic fund tranfers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government believes that money laundering constitutes a very serious problem. I can assure the hon. member that we will continue to use the most recent technology and the most efficient methods to fight this curse.
The government already took some initiatives. For example, Bill C-61, concerning proceeds of crime, recently came into force. This new law makes it illegal to launder the proceeds of crime, it allows duly authorized police officers to search and seize any property suspected of being illegally obtained, and it relieves the banks of all responsibility when disclosing information on activities they believe to be related to money laundering. Also in accordance with this Act, criminal assets can be confiscated.
Our government has also passed a law concerning the implementation of cooperation treaties in criminal matters in order to further cooperation between Canadian judicial authorities and their foreign counterparts. The Treaty on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters between Canada and the United States was concluded, ratified and came into effect on January 24, 1990. We have signed similar agreements with Australia and the United Kingdom, and negociations with other countries, including the Group of Seven, except Japan, are going very well.
In December 1988, Canada signed the UN Convention of Illicit Drug and Psychotropic Substance Trafficking, which puts great emphasis on international cooperation for tracking down and confiscating revenues from such trafficking.
The Bank for International Settlements has also examined the question of money laundering. In January 1989, Canada and other countries represented on the Cooke Committee of the Bank for International Settlements signed a document entitled "Prevention of the use of the banking system for the laundering of proceeds of crime". This agreement provides for a better identification of clients, a greater compliance with foreign laws, cooperation with judicial authorities and adequate training of people involved in the financial system.
At the Economic Summit held in Paris in July 1989, heads of states vowed to fight against drug trafficking, insisting that financial measures would be a concrete and encouraging approach towards this goal. They decided to

March 12, 1990
Adjournment Debate
create a financial task force composed of representatives of countries participating in the summit and of other industrialized countries. Canada has taken an active part in the work of this task force, whose mandate is to evaluate the results of the cooperation measures already taken in the fight against the use of the banking system for the laundering of money and to examine other preventive measures in this area. Members of the task force have met several times and their recommendations will be made public soon.
On February 9, 1990, the Advisory Committee on money laundering created under the National AntiDrug Strategy held its first meeting. This committee's mandate is to review our mechanism to prevent money laundering, to identify areas where improvements could be made and to inform the government on the benefits of the different alternatives to deal with money laundering. Another mandate of the Committee is to act as an advisory link between industry and govemement in technical matters and to publicize the steps taken by Canadian financial institutions.
At its first meeting, committee members took the opportunity to unanimously endorse a statement affirming their complete support for the fight against money laundering and undertook to keep all the accounting records on financial transactions needed by the RCMP and other police forces to investigate and take moneylaundering cases to court. In its coming meetings, the Committee will be asked to deal with various ways to fight money laundering. The decisions on solutions to the problem of money laundering and their implementation will be made in the light of the Committee's recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to speak on behalf of veterans with respect to the recent budget. I am speaking on behalf of veterans not just because I am the veterans' affairs critic or because I am associate defence critic or because I have spent most of a lifetime in uniform myself
but because I want to put on the record the concerns that have been expressed to me.
I do not want to mince words and I do not want to play politics with this particular issue, but the fact is that some veterans will have to pay more and some veterans will lose specific benefits as a result of the over-all budget. I appreciate what the hon. minister has said in that regard. He should also know that tremendous representation is being made to me as the critic. It is very important to represent the views of those veterans who are concerned about what is happening.
I said I served in uniform, Mr. Speaker, but I did not serve in war and I was pleased that I did not have to. Shortly after I was bom, in September, 1939, World War II was upon us and our country was passing through what was described by many to be the shadow and the storm of war. This dark hour was illuminated by the white light of human courage. The bitterness of suffering was alleviated by the inspiration of patriotism, and the dark cloud overhead carried a silver lining that foretold the brightness of a coming dawn. That brightness was the 1.75 million Canadian men and women who saw service in wars in this country.
I use the beginning of World War II as an example. I can also use World War I as an example and I think I can do no better than to refer to a veteran who happens to be in my riding. I know him very well. He is 93 years of age and he served in Gallipoli and at Beaumont-Hamel. This gentleman's name is Mr. Ronald Dunn. He has just written a letter in which he points out that he is 93 and that he is paying $240 a month but expects that is going to change before too long. He goes on to say that: "you are now tiying to save money by raising our rent to $420 a month."
There is a rationale, if you look at it as a chartered accountant or as a financial expert, which I suppose could make sense. I am not too sure it makes a lot of sense to Mr. Dunn who has a limited income and who now sees his rent being doubled with, to my understanding at this point, not much of a chance of phasing in.
To add to the feeling that is behind this, I want to quote some of the things that Mr. Dunn described from when he was serving as a young boy in Beaumont-Hamel, where as many people remember most of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment was wiped out, and in Gallipo-
March 12, 1990

li. I have only seen movies of Gallipoli and Mr. Dunn's description is very vivid.
He said: "We had a hard time of it, no question about it. You had to be iron to stand it. In the trenches were millions of black flies and crawlers swarming over the men's bodies. There was very little to eat. Toward the latter part of November, the rain came and filled the trenches. Following this, the snow fell and the freezing temperatures came. The men suffered from dysentery, diarrhea and lice. Some men died while others had to be taken from service to recuperate. These are the things the men had to face, besides fighting the Turks".
I could go on. I hope I have left a vivid thought of what our veterans went through. I am sure the minister will be happy to know I am not going to go into a long dissertation about how heartless and callous this particular cut was. I appreciate the position the minister must have been in when he had to give up his share of the budget because I understand that everybody was told they had to give something.
That is fair enough. But I think you draw a line at a certain point in time where you cannot give up something. In the case of veterans who are not represented except by politicians in the House of Commons, they cannot defend themselves. Thus it is up to the opposition to make the point that this was not a smart move. Morally, it was not a smart move in the sense of care. Quite frankly, I do not think it was even a politically smart move.
I want to quote now from a song or a verse. The members in the House may recall there was a song with the chorus: "And the band played Marching Matilda. I remember it. It is a very striking song and a very striking poem about a young boy who served at Gallipoli and who came back home to live. He had no legs when he got home. When he sat in his house and remembered all these things, he wished he had not lived. But he did write the song in which he talked about his joining as a boy and the hardships such as those which Mr. Dunn went through.
The last verse is very vivid. He talks about his memories now, as an old man. The last verse goes something like this: "And now every year I sit on my porch and I
Adjournment Debate
watch the parade pass before me. I watch my old comrades, how proudly they march, reliving their deeds of past glories. I watch my old comrades, tired, stiff and sore. They are forgotten heroes of a forgotten war. And the young people ask, 'What are they marching for'? And I ask myself the same question".
Mr. Speaker, they are marching to remind us that we have had peace, liberty and freedom for so long that we may forget that the price of that was blood. It is not any accident that the colour of the poppy is red. They are marching to remind us of their comrades who did not come home. They are marching to remind us, I suppose more than anything, to pay attention to letters like the one that we got from Mr. Ronald Dunn from Bonavista, who served at Gallipoli and Beaumont-Hamel. He ends up his letter by saying: "You are going to charge now $420 a month. Is this not a strange way of showing your appreciation for what we did? The money you save, will it be worth hurting us again? Haven't we suffered enough during and since the war? It seems to me as if we have to pay our debt all over again".
That is what we are marching for. I am quoting what the man himself said.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to thank the opposition critic for, once again, allowing me the opportunity to put some facts on the table for the public and to get the facts on the record as I did in the House on Friday.
I am finding that the more the veterans hear of the reasons for the changes, the more they understand why the changes were made. The Dominion President of the Royal Canadian Legion and the Chairman of the National Council of Veterans Association consider the charges we will be making for board and lodging to be fair and reasonable. They know the facts. I think it is important that we try to explain that tonight.
The changes in the charges for room and board are in the interest of ensuring equality of treatment among our veterans. More than 70 per cent of all non-pensioned veterans are presently paying $8 a day for room and board. The other 30 per cent are paying nothing because of inconsistent regulations. A lot of veterans have objected to this unequal treatment, and rightly so.

March 12, 1990
Adjournment Debate
On April 1, 1990, everyone will pay the $240 a month. Every veteran will be treated the same in every province of Canada. I think the veterans would appreciate that. Once more, I must emphasize that all those in an institution because of war-related disabilities pay nothing now and are going to pay nothing after April 1, 1990, or in the future.
When the rates rise in April, 1991, they will be the lowest rates in any jurisdiction in Canada; $14 a day for room, meals, laundry, recreation and nursing care, and all the rest that they receive. That is nothing close to the $130 a day it really costs on average to maintain a veteran in a chronic care bed in Canada. That is $4,000 a month, or almost $50,000 a year.
I repeat the promise that veterans will not be worse off financially should they have to move out of their own homes and into an institution. Our income protection features will take care of that.
With regard to the Veterans Independence Program, I again appreciate the opportunity to tell the House with pride that our VIP payments have increased by 60 per cent this year alone. They will double in another four years. That is hardly what I call scrimping on our veterans.
I also want again to put to rest any fears veterans might have over the consequences of the removal of heavy housekeeping from our lengthy list of services under VIP. Should there be any legitimate health and safety requirement on the part of an individual for the provision of a service presently available under heavy housekeeping, we will make sure that particular service in reinstated.
I believe that even the hon. critic for the opposition will agree that no veteran need be alarmed by the removal of this one item from an extremely generous and far-sighted catalogue of services. I certainly hope he realizes that the changes which have been made are in the interest of fairness, equity and justice for our veteran community.
As Doug Fisher, who was a member of Parliament in this House and a noted columnist now, himself a veteran put it: "No nation has treated those who served in its wars more generously than Canada". That was true yesterday, it is true now and will be true in the future.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to elaborate on my question of February 7 to the Prime Minister. My question, which the minister responsible for ACOA addressed on the Prime Minister's behalf, dealt with the so-called rescue plan worked out by the federal and Nova Scotia governments with National Sea Products for the fish plant in Canso.
This agreement, which was made without consultation with the people of Canso or the fish plant workers there, essentially contributed some $3 million to National Sea Products, in return for which the company was going to keep the plant open at a bare minimum, employing some 150 workers for four months of the year, after which they would give up their work for another 150 for four months of the year and then they would all go on unemployment insurance. This is a reduction from an 800-person workforce.
The trawler port was to be closed and fish was to be trucked in to Canso. One element of the plan was to allow the company to not pay the severance benefits which were to be paid to workers, because previously the plant was to be shut down. The bail-out essentially allowed National Sea Products to improve its assets in Canso and to allow a certain portion of the workers to draw unemployment insurance benefits. As one of the local commentators described it: "If this is a rescue plan, heaven help the town they decide to abandon".
The deal was rejected by the labour unions, the representatives of the fish plant workers and the trawler-men, and it has been rejected as a cruel hoax by the people of Canso. More recently it has been repudiated publicly by none other than the Premier of Nova Scotia himself, which led many to wonder after reading the comments he made to the press two weeks ago if he was, in fact, awake when the so-called rescue plan was being worked out.
Now we have a new Minister of Fisheries, who began in a promising way by visiting Canso and who won high praise in the local press for doing so. He has since become, however, infected with the disease of his predecessor which is touting the company line and saying: "The problem is too many fishermen chasing too few fish, and there is nothing more that the government can do about it".
March 12, 1990

The implied message, of course, is: "Sorry, Canso, but this government does not believe that you have a future in the fishery. You will simply have to go the way of Schefferville." That is not good enough. It is not good enough for the fish plant workers in Canso. It is certainly not good enough for the trawler workers in Canso whose port will be closed as a result of this deal. That is the point that I want to address in the remainder of these remarks.
The minister for ACOA replied to my supplementary on February 7 by saying that I was advocating what he called an entirely new concept to fisheries port quotas. This is a good place to set the record straight on what I was advocating.
In fact, it is quite unnecessary to institute a whole new concept of fisheries management in order to satisfy the simple basic requirement that Canso trawlermen be allowed to land their fish in Canso. It merely requires that the Minister of Fisheries exercise his responsibilities under the Fisheries Act.
Section 7 of the Fisheries Act states subject to Section 2 the Minister of Fisheries may, in his absolute discretion, wherever the exclusive right of fishing does not already exist by law, issue or authorize to be issued leases or licences for fisheries or fishing wherever situated or carried on.
Under the enterprise allocation program, which is one of the components of the allocation of fish and fish licensing and which determines the allocation for offshore vessels, the minister can and in fact does attach conditions to the issuance of enterprise allocations.
In fact, he specifies the kinds of vessels and the number of vessels which can be fished under the licences. He can and does specify the fish that can be caught and where they can be caught, and the fishing gear.
He specifies a number of other matters. In the time remaining, the point I want to come to is that what is required of this Minister of Fisheries is simply that he attach a condition to the enterprise allocation which would oblige the fishing trawlers that fish out of Canso to land their fish in Canso, rather than land their fish somewhere else and truck it into Canso. That is entirely consistent with the Enterprise Allocation Program. The minister can do it. It is one of the simple recommendations which would preserve the Canso plant. It is the
Adjournment Debate
form of leadership which has been conspicuously lacking in this government.
We should not forget that when the Liberal government restructured the fishery back in 1982 it had a lot to say about National Sea Products and helped that company out in order to allow a fish plant in Canso to be maintained viable. What we need from this government is a commitment to communities such as Canso and to use a little bit of imagination in coming up with a program to save communities which have no other alternative but to remain in the fishery. That is what I am counting on the new Minister of Fisheries to provide.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by responding to the remarks the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso made with respect to the closing of the plant at Canso in the province of Nova Scotia.
I want to remind him and the people of Canso that when National Sea Products Limited announced the closure of the plant in December of 1989, there were to be no jobs at all. As a result of negotiations by the federal government, by the government of Nova Scotia with National Sea, a new arrangement was made whereby 150 jobs to be shared by 300 plant workers were created and were to be continued on a long-term basis.
Nobody suggested that this was an ultimate solution, but what it did was breathe hope and some life into what otherwise would have been a closed fish plant.
I want to remind the member, too, that in 1970 this same difficulty occurred when Acadia Fisheries closed down in Canso and the plant was left unoperated. It was only when the Government of Nova Scotia and other governments intervened to again breathe some life into the fish plant that a new life was created and the fish plant continued until this latest crisis.
I want to remind the member that there is some passage of time that has to be taken into account when one is being so critical of these attempts to revive what is obviously, by all agreement, a difficult situation.
Everyone has said since the beginning of this difficulty that there are no magic solutions. You do not need to take my word for that. That was the subject of a column in the Toronto Globe and Mail by Jeffrey Simpson who commented on the emergency debate on the Atlantic fisheries held in December of 1989. He pointed out that rhetoric provides no solution. He said:

March 12, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Rhetoric aside, the opposition's major alternative seemed to be to force National Sea Products-to spare the closed plants by spreading fish supplies around. How that could and should be done with a 1990 catch 45,000 tonnes below that of 1989 remained unaddressed, for the good reason that there is no answer.
That is the problem. There are no magic solutions. Do not take my word for it. It has been confirmed by a great many experts.
Let me deal very briefly with the matter of community quotas, or port quotas as the member called them. This arrangement has been dismissed by his own colleague in the Senate, Senator Michael Kirby, who was the author of the task force on Atlantic fisheries back in 1982. He said:
The community quota scheme is completely irrational from an economic point of view since it implies, first, that all plants must be subsidized, and second, that capacity adjustment would not take place anywhere.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is not the government that is turning down community quotas or port quotas, it is his own
colleague in the Senate of Canada advising against it. Notwithstanding that, the government is looking at this as it is looking at all solutions.
Let me end on a positive note. The Prime Minister of Canada was in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on March 6, 1990, and he reiterated his promise that there would be an assistance package for the Atlantic fishery. It will not just help Canso, it will help Lockeport and all the other areas that are suffering under this current plight in the Atlantic fisheries.
Let us get positive about this thing. Let us come to the House of Commons with solutions, not with empty rhetoric.
